title: PX4 SITL MAVSDK test seg faulting
author: MaEtUgR
body:
I saw [seemingly random PX4 mavsdk tests in the PX4 CI seg fault](https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/pull/25261#issuecomment-3586520441) and went into a rabbit hole to find out why.

After managing to run the tests against a simple SIH simulation instance https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/compare/main...maetugr/sih-ci I was able to reproduce seg faults every now and then locally.
I then removed this line from Catch2: https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/blob/main/test/mavsdk_tests/catch2/catch.hpp#L8027 which prevents it from capturing the seg fault and screwing up debugging.
Then figuring out all the commands to run manually such that the python invocator can't capture the seg fault but I can do that with gdb:
```
DONT_RUN=1 make px4_sitl mavsdk_tests
PX4_SIM_MODEL=sihsim_quadx PX4_SIM_SPEED_FACTOR=10 build/px4_sitl_default/bin/px4 build/px4_sitl_default/etc -s etc/init.d-posix/rcS -t test_data -d
gdb --args build/px4_sitl_default/mavsdk_tests/mavsdk_tests --url udpin://0.0.0.0:14540 --speed-factor 10 "Takeoff and hold position"
```

In gdb I used:
```
catch signal SIGSEGV
run
```

and get the following output:

As far as I can tell I narrowed it down to MAVSDK 3.11.1 which probably not by coincidence was updated just recently in:
https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot/commit/ff06a206d1a8903f0c275ac4fc5b0fe809ef7269

I haven't investigated in detail what causes the problem but it looks related to events 🤔 Honestly I feel a bit lost so if I could get any help that might lead us to a solution sooner👀

title: Mavsdk and Ros2 causes nondescript segfault
author: nbingham1
body:
Minimal example of node that tries to use Mavsdk. This example works if mavsdk is commented out or ros2 is not used. If Mavsdk is initialized at all in a Ros2 node, it causes a segfault.

```bash
~/workspace/px4_mission_service$ find *
CMakeLists.txt
src
src/node.cpp
~/workspace/px4_mission_service$ cat src/node.cpp 
#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include <mavsdk/mavsdk.h>

struct Px4MissionService : public rclcpp::Node {
	mavsdk::Mavsdk sdk;

	Px4MissionService() 
		: rclcpp::Node("px4_mission_service"),
		  sdk(mavsdk::Mavsdk::Configuration{mavsdk::ComponentType::GroundStation}) 
	{}
};

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
	rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
	rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<Px4MissionService>());
	rclcpp::shutdown();
	return 0;
}

find_package(MAVSDK REQUIRED)

add_executable(mission_service src/node.cpp)

Ok, looks like the problem is symbols clashing because the default is public.

This is fixed in main by https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/2824 but we might have to do some backported version of it for v3.
Just released [v3.17.0](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/releases/tag/v3.17.0). Give it a try!

**Investigation summary for #2852**

The root cause is **symbol leakage** from `libmavsdk.so`. MAVSDK statically links OpenSSL, tinyxml2, and curl into its shared library, but those symbols remain globally visible. When loaded alongside ROS2 (which uses FastRTPS -> OpenSSL/tinyxml2), the dynamic linker resolves FastRTPS's calls to MAVSDK's bundled copies, causing ABI mismatches and the segfault.

Confirmed via `LD_DEBUG=bindings`:
```
binding file /opt/ros/jazzy/lib/libfastrtps.so.2.14 [0] to /lib/libmavsdk.so.3 [0]: normal symbol `OPENSSL_init_crypto'
binding file /opt/ros/jazzy/lib/libfastrtps.so.2.14 [0] to /lib/libmavsdk.so.3 [0]: normal symbol `_ZN8tinyxml211XMLDocumentC1E...'
```

**What we tried:**
1. Backported PR #2824 (`-fvisibility=hidden` + `MAVSDK_PUBLIC` annotations) to v3 -> branch `v3-symbol-visibility`
2. Built a .deb from that branch and tested in Docker with the reproducer from this issue

**Result:** Still crashes. `-fvisibility=hidden` only affects symbols compiled with that flag. The statically-linked third-party `.a` files (OpenSSL, tinyxml2, curl) were built without it, so their symbols are still exported from `libmavsdk.so`.

**Next step:** Add a **linker version script** to the shared library build. This tells the linker to hide all symbols except the MAVSDK public API, regardless of how the static libraries were compiled:

```
# libmavsdk.version
{
  global:
    _ZN6mavsdk*;   # mavsdk:: namespace
    _ZNK6mavsdk*;  # const methods in mavsdk::
    extern "C++" {
      "mavsdk::*";
    };
  local:
    *;
};
```

Applied in CMake with:
```cmake
set_target_properties(mavsdk PROPERTIES
    LINK_FLAGS "-Wl,--version-script=${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/libmavsdk.version"
)
```

This needs to go into both v3 and main. The Docker reproducer is in `issue_2852/` in the repo.

**Reproducer:** `issue_2852/Dockerfile` (based on `ros:jazzy`, installs MAVSDK .deb, builds minimal ROS2+MAVSDK node)

Here is the dockerfile:

```
FROM ros:jazzy

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    gdb \
    wget \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install MAVSDK 3.17.0 .deb
RUN wget -q https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/releases/download/v3.17.0/libmavsdk-dev_3.17.0_ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb \
    && dpkg -i libmavsdk-dev_3.17.0_ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb \
    && rm libmavsdk-dev_3.17.0_ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb

# Create the reproducer project
RUN mkdir -p /workspace/px4_mission_service/src
COPY node.cpp /workspace/px4_mission_service/src/node.cpp
COPY CMakeLists.txt /workspace/px4_mission_service/CMakeLists.txt

# Build the reproducer
WORKDIR /workspace/px4_mission_service
RUN bash -c "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && \
    mkdir build && cd build && \
    cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug .. && \
    make -j$(nproc)"

CMD ["./build/mission_service"]
```

**Investigation summary for #2852**

The root cause is **symbol leakage** from `libmavsdk.so`. MAVSDK statically links OpenSSL, tinyxml2, and curl into its shared library, but those symbols remain globally visible. When loaded alongside ROS2 (which uses FastRTPS -> OpenSSL/tinyxml2), the dynamic linker resolves FastRTPS's calls to MAVSDK's bundled copies, causing ABI mismatches and the segfault.

Confirmed via `LD_DEBUG=bindings`:
```
binding file /opt/ros/jazzy/lib/libfastrtps.so.2.14 [0] to /lib/libmavsdk.so.3 [0]: normal symbol `OPENSSL_init_crypto'
binding file /opt/ros/jazzy/lib/libfastrtps.so.2.14 [0] to /lib/libmavsdk.so.3 [0]: normal symbol `_ZN8tinyxml211XMLDocumentC1E...'
```

**What we tried:**
1. Backported PR #2824 (`-fvisibility=hidden` + `MAVSDK_PUBLIC` annotations) to v3 -> branch `v3-symbol-visibility`
2. Built a .deb from that branch and tested in Docker with the reproducer from this issue

**Result:** Still crashes. `-fvisibility=hidden` only affects symbols compiled with that flag. The statically-linked third-party `.a` files (OpenSSL, tinyxml2, curl) were built without it, so their symbols are still exported from `libmavsdk.so`.

**Next step:** Add a **linker version script** to the shared library build. This tells the linker to hide all symbols except the MAVSDK public API, regardless of how the static libraries were compiled:

```
# libmavsdk.version
{
  global:
    _ZN6mavsdk*;   # mavsdk:: namespace
    _ZNK6mavsdk*;  # const methods in mavsdk::
    extern "C++" {
      "mavsdk::*";
    };
  local:
    *;
};
```

Applied in CMake with:
```cmake
set_target_properties(mavsdk PROPERTIES
    LINK_FLAGS "-Wl,--version-script=${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/libmavsdk.version"
)
```

This needs to go into both v3 and main. The Docker reproducer is in `issue_2852/` in the repo.

**Reproducer:** `issue_2852/Dockerfile` (based on `ros:jazzy`, installs MAVSDK .deb, builds minimal ROS2+MAVSDK node)

Here is the dockerfile:

```
FROM ros:jazzy

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    gdb \
    wget \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install MAVSDK 3.17.0 .deb
RUN wget -q https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/releases/download/v3.17.0/libmavsdk-dev_3.17.0_ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb \
    && dpkg -i libmavsdk-dev_3.17.0_ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb \
    && rm libmavsdk-dev_3.17.0_ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb

# Create the reproducer project
RUN mkdir -p /workspace/px4_mission_service/src
COPY node.cpp /workspace/px4_mission_service/src/node.cpp
COPY CMakeLists.txt /workspace/px4_mission_service/CMakeLists.txt

# Build the reproducer
WORKDIR /workspace/px4_mission_service
RUN bash -c "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && \
    mkdir build && cd build && \
    cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug .. && \
    make -j$(nproc)"

CMD ["./build/mission_service"]
```

Yep :) I can confirm that the branch fixes the segfault

Thanks!

> Ideally it would use system provided protobuf if available, unless there's a particular reason for using a separate compile, to save compile time and other problems like this.

The way it works is that the `MAVSDK` project finds its dependencies using [`find_package`](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/command/find_package.html). So if you want to deal with the dependencies manually (which is perfectly fine), you should run with [`-DSUPERBUILD=OFF`](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/develop/CMakeLists.txt#L5). The reason why we default to `-DSUPERBUILD=ON` is that most of our users don't know or don't want to deal with the dependencies themselves. Other reasons for having the superbuild at all is that we sometimes need to build our dependencies for some platforms (e.g. manylinux), and we sometimes need to patch them for other platforms.

What the superbuild does is conceptually quite easy:

a. It builds the dependencies separately and installs them ([by default](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/develop/CMakeLists.txt#L11)) in `${PROJECT_BINARY_DIR}/third_party/install`
b. It sets `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` to that install directory for mavsdk
c. It builds MAVSDK

Which means that if MAVSDK doesn't find the dependency in `${PROJECT_BINARY_DIR}/third_party/install`, it will look for it on your system. But we don't have options to enable/disable each dependency separately: either you enable the superbuild, or you don't. If you want to do something in-between (i.e. have some dependencies on your system, and some built by our scripts), please feel free to do that! It is not super complicated, but you have to do it manually.

## Bug Description
The `mavlink_direct` plugin's `subscribe_message` method does not properly filter messages when a specific `message_name` is provided. Instead of receiving only the requested message type, subscribers receive ALL message types.

## Expected Behavior
When subscribing with a specific message name (e.g., `message_name="HEARTBEAT"`), the subscriber should only receive messages of that type.

## Actual Behavior
Subscribers receive ALL message types regardless of the filter specified. The `message_name` parameter is completely ignored.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Start MAVSDK server v3.10.1
2. Connect via gRPC and use the mavlink_direct service
3. Call `SubscribeMessage` with `message_name="HEARTBEAT"`
4. Observe that you receive all message types (ATTITUDE, TIMESYNC, GPS_RAW_INT, etc.)

## Test Results
Testing with a Python gRPC client shows:
- **No filter (empty string)**: Correctly receives all 34 message types
- **Filter "HEARTBEAT"**: Incorrectly receives all 34 message types (should only receive HEARTBEAT)
- **Filter "TIMESYNC"**: Incorrectly receives all 34 message types (should only receive TIMESYNC)
- **Filter "ATTITUDE"**: Incorrectly receives all 34 message types (should only receive ATTITUDE)

## Root Cause Analysis
Looking at the code in `mavlink_direct_impl.cpp`:
- The `subscribe_message` method stores the `message_name` filter
- It registers with `SystemImpl::register_libmav_message_handler`
- However, when messages arrive, they're forwarded to ALL subscribers regardless of their individual filters
- The stored `message_name` is never actually used to filter messages before invoking callbacks

## Environment
- MAVSDK version: v3.10.1
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04
- Connection: gRPC on port 50051
- Test vehicle: PX4 SITL

## Workaround
Until fixed, users must manually filter messages in their client code:
```python
# Subscribe to all messages (empty filter)
request = mavlink_direct_pb2.SubscribeMessageRequest(message_name="")
responses = stub.SubscribeMessage(request)

for response in responses:
    if response.HasField('message'):
        msg = response.message
        # Manual filtering
        if msg.message_name == "HEARTBEAT":
            # Process only HEARTBEAT messages
            process_message(msg)
```

## Impact
This bug makes the filtering feature completely non-functional, forcing all clients to receive and process all messages, which can significantly impact performance in high-frequency telemetry scenarios.

comments.body: Thanks for the report. That doesn't sound right indeed!

Hm, I can't reproduce this.

So, the subscription happens here:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/872f17c566b3099520c4de7336977fde6f6ce84f/src/mavsdk/plugins/mavlink_direct/mavlink_direct_impl.cpp#L148-L149

which goes here:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/872f17c566b3099520c4de7336977fde6f6ce84f/src/mavsdk/core/system_impl.cpp#L165-L174

And the filtering happens here:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/872f17c566b3099520c4de7336977fde6f6ce84f/src/mavsdk/core/system_impl.cpp#L140-L145

And last I checked it was correct in my Python example. What am I missing?

Hi @julianoes,

Thanks for looking into this. I tested with v3.10.1 and can still reproduce the issue. I think I found where the problem might be.

The filtering you pointed to in `system_impl.cpp` works correctly:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/872f17c566b3099520c4de7336977fde6f6ce84f/src/mavsdk/core/system_impl.cpp#L140-L145

However, the issue seems to be in how `mavlink_direct_impl.cpp` handles the callbacks after filtering. When subscribing, it registers this handler:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/872f17c566b3099520c4de7336977fde6f6ce84f/src/mavsdk/plugins/mavlink_direct/mavlink_direct_impl.cpp#L148-L166

The callback at line 150-163 receives the correctly filtered message, but then at line 161 it calls:

```cpp
_message_subscriptions.queue(direct_message, [this](const auto& func) {
    _system_impl->call_user_callback(func);
});
```

This `_message_subscriptions.queue()` broadcasts the message to ALL subscribers of MavlinkDirect, not just the ones who subscribed to that specific message type. The `_message_subscriptions` is a single `CallbackList` that doesn't differentiate between what each subscriber originally requested.

So the flow is:
1. User A subscribes to "HEARTBEAT"  
2. User B subscribes to "GPS_RAW_INT"
3. Both callbacks get registered in the same `_message_subscriptions` list
4. When a HEARTBEAT arrives, it passes the filter and triggers User A's handler
5. But that handler broadcasts the HEARTBEAT to both User A and User B

Here's my test output with gRPC client against v3.10.1:
```
Subscribing to: "HEARTBEAT"
Received: ATTITUDE
Received: GLOBAL_POSITION_INT  
Received: HIGHRES_IMU
...
```

I could provide a minimal reproduction script if that would help. Let me know if I'm misunderstanding how the CallbackList is supposed to work!
As Claude would say "[You're absolutely right!](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/3382)" Thanks for looking into it. Fix coming.
Fix coming with https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/2650 and v3.10.2.
@ayatim let me know if this is fixed for you.
Thanks @julianoes, all good here

title: Document/support process for using custom mavlink dialect
author: Ryanf55
body:
I want to add a few custom mavlink messages for my own dialect, not part of upstream, and develop without having to commit and push to a repository.

Right now, mavlink is brought in through ExternalProject_add like so:
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/5b66d5fb8e2032b9f24dc08867e950b0b32ec82e/third_party/mavlink/CMakeLists.txt#L32-L45



The URL is hard-coded to upstream
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/5b66d5fb8e2032b9f24dc08867e950b0b32ec82e/third_party/mavlink/CMakeLists.txt#L34

Then, for a local build, mavlink is built and installed, so that its config file is on disk.
This allows it to be found through find_package:
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/5b66d5fb8e2032b9f24dc08867e950b0b32ec82e/src/mavsdk/core/CMakeLists.txt#L4

For some reason, regardless of the setting for the MAVLINK_DIALECT, it does not get affect the command here:
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/5b66d5fb8e2032b9f24dc08867e950b0b32ec82e/src/mavsdk/core/CMakeLists.txt#L27-L39


I want to

* Add a new local mavlink XML dialect, say my_custom.xml
* Get MAVSDK to also generate that dialect in addition to the normal dialect
* Use those new messages to send custom packets via mavsdk

Can we either document or add support for mavlink to be brought in through a submodule, fetchcontent, or how to build/install mavlink on the system that does not rely on merging stuff upstream first? Perhaps we can support a way where mavlink on the system can be used.

In mavlink:
```
cmake -B build -DMAVLINK_DIALECT=MyCustomDialect
cmake --build build
cmake --install build --prefix install
```
Which generates the following header (as expected)
```
/home/ryan/Dev/mavlink/install/include/mavlink/MyCustomDialect/mavlink_msg_my_custom_dialect_toy.h
```
Then, when building MAVSDK, perhaps we can allow a user to add "/path/to/mavlink/install" to the CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH and use that version instead of pulling from upstream.

Trying this today results in the following error:
```
gmake[2]: *** No rule to make target 'third_party/install/include/mavlink/message_definitions/v1.0/ardupilotmega.xml', needed by 'src/mavsdk/core/embedded_mavlink_xml.h'.  Stop.
gmake[1]: *** [CMakeFiles/Makefile2:910: src/mavsdk/core/CMakeFiles/generate_core_mavlink_xml_header.dir/all] Error 2
gmake: *** [Makefile:136: all] Error 2
```
I spent a fair bit of time trying to understand this step of the build system but don't know how to proceed.

answer_comments.body: Well the dependencies are built by the superbuild, so it shouldn't be too hard to find them. Here they are: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/third_party/CMakeLists.txt.

> I'm already submitting patches to upstream libraries.

We've upstreamed quite a few patches over the years. Some of them were just not accepted. For instance TinyXML did not want to support older CMake versions at all. Now maybe our patch is obsolete (do we still support CMake 3.10.2? That was for Ubuntu 18.04 which is EOL, so I'm guessing we can just remove this patch 🤔.

> From what I can tell, there is no place that MAVSDK actually checks out and builds TinyXML with superbuild disabled.

Because that's the whole point of a superbuild, isn't it? Either the superbuild builds the dependencies, or you handle them yourself 😇.

> Instead, it builds the superbuild, then re-uses the built dependencies again with superbuild disabled, which isn't really a fair build.

I don't understand what you mean here. If you disable the superbuild, it doesn't build the dependencies, period. It will still run `find_package` for them, and it is your responsibility to provide them.

> All the patches that MAVSDK is doing to upstream libraries need to get applied too.

Only those that apply to your platform and are necessary for your build, but yeah. Again, if you don't use our helpers, it's your responsibility. Always better when patches are not needed, and I'm happy whenever we can remove one 😊.

> Saying that we need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect

You don't need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect. There are many other ways, e.g.:

1. You can fork the repo and modify the two lines you need to modify in the MAVLink helper in third_party. That's literally a 2 lines change.
2. You can run the MAVSDK configure step with superbuild enabled, have your own step that replaces the locally-installed MAVLink with your custom one, and then proceed with the build step.

> large hurdle due to the large amount of undocumented customizations, patches, and other oddities done.

I don't know if this is the goal, but this kind of value judgment (and it happened in other messages as well) sounds offensive to me. Remember that I am doing this for free, in my free time. And unless you're paying @julianoes, he's doing it for free as well.

> Would you consider an approach of a hybrid superbuild that allows some packages available through find_package

Most definitely not, it is out of the question for me. You are complaining that our build is "odd", and in the next sentence you ask that we made it even more complicated just for your specific use-case. Either you use the superbuild, or you deal with the dependencies manually. And "dealing with the dependencies manually" means that you can just copy-paste all our helpers and use that. If you want to do it differently (in docker, in a shell script, in a python script, with a package manager), you're free to do so.

> At minimum. it appears safe to remove our third_party/tinyxml2/cmake-3.10.2.patch

It does indeed, thanks for the PR! 🚀 

> What I am getting at would that it would be helpful if there was a shell script, dockerfile, or CI file

From my point of view, it's all documented in code in https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/tree/main/third_party. I agree that the superbuild makes it harder to understand, but if you look at the individual CMakeLists for the dependencies, it's all really just like I describe in [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/).

Really, those contains exactly everything we need (including patches and compilation options) for the dependencies.

> would you consider making the URL and hash CMake options so I can supply those arguments at configure time rather than needing a fork? 

If you find a way to do it (I haven't looked into it), I say why not. My concern is that the superbuild scripts will make it convoluted. Again that is why I am now in favour of keeping the dependencies clearly separated from the project (again, [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/)) rather than having CMake build the dependencies as part of the project's configure step. This said, if we only provided helpers you would still have to somehow patch the MAVLink helper, so it would be similar to a fork/patch.

I would like to note that some of the "oddities" you find currently came exactly like this: "it makes it easier for the users if we do this automatically". So the happy path is just one command, but under the hood it adds complexity. That's why our CMake configure step requires python, for instance, because MAVLink needs it.

I am a bit of a purist here and came to think that we should simplify our build and delegate more to the users (making it their responsibility to understand how to build the dependencies, for instance). @julianoes is more pragmatic there, and I trust his judgement 😬.

> Perhaps it would help if I demonstrate what that would look like?

Why not, you would have to convince @julianoes here 😊. My way would be to remove the superbuild and just provide the helpers, and have users build like I describe [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/). I know e.g. gRPC offers some kind of hybrid way and I personally find that it just adds complexity.

comments.body: Before going into building your own custom dialect, may I ask if you considered using the MavlinkDirect plugin? It allows you to "inject" your own messages at runtime without having to rebuild MAVSDK.

> Before going into building your own custom dialect, may I ask if you considered using the MavlinkDirect plugin? It allows you to "inject" your own messages at runtime without having to rebuild MAVSDK.

Good question.

We need to make the XML regardless so that the tooling on the other components of our system speaks the same language.
We're going to want our GCS to be able to decode the data, our autopilot, our companion computer, and the developer tooling for log analysis, wireshark debugging, etc. Not all of them use MAVSDK. We are expecting a lot of custom messages, so we need something easy to keep changing.

The MavlinkDirect plugin approach could be an alternative, but I am concerned about the stability of it given the caution in the wiki.
Is this ready for production applications? Is it safe for a "mission critical" interface yet? The lack of enum support is annoying. At minimum, I'd try to get MAVSDK to import the message from an XML dialect rather than hard-coding the message definition in the C++ source code.

> Is this ready for production applications? Is it safe for a "mission critical" interface yet? 

Try it out and decide for yourself. The API is there to stay, maybe it'll change slightly but I think the design makes sense.
Does it have bugs, maybe. If you discover one, let me know and I'll try to fix it. If it's urgent and important, consider [sponsoring me](https://github.com/sponsors/julianoes) to move it up on my todo list.

> The lack of enum support is annoying.

It's a runtime thing, so there won't be native enums. That being said, we might be able to make enums using strings work. It'll just take some implementation. Again, up to you to contribute or convince me.
Are you open to improving compile time support for custom dialects?

> The lack of enum support is annoying.

By the way, I just checked and it looks like libmav (or our fork libmavlike) that we use for the xml parsing seems to have some support for enums, so it's a matter of integrating that into our API.

> Are you open to improving compile time support for custom dialects?

Like what? Not sure I understand what you mean.

> > Are you open to improving compile time support for custom dialects?
> 
> Like what? Not sure I understand what you mean.

I would like to point MAVSDK to my own local copy of the mavlink repo and when I compile mavsdk, have all dialects in my local fork built.
Currently, MAVSDK fetches and builds mavlink through ExternalProject_add which requires you to commit/push any changes to upstream.
I'd prefer an alternative approach such as `add_subdirectory` with a git submodule, or something like FetchContent , or even pulling in mavlink through find_package which any of these would allow you to easily change to a private fork of mavlink with custom messages and iterate quickly without having to commit/push.

This makes our custom messages driven off an XML file rather than JSON with compile time alignment with other tools in the ecosystem.

> I'd prefer an alternative approach such as add_subdirectory with a git submodule, or something like FetchContent , or even pulling in mavlink through find_package which any of these would allow you to easily change to a private fork of mavlink with custom messages and iterate quickly without having to commit/push.

We already have that: all our dependencies are pulled with `find_package`. We have a convoluted superbuild (I can say it because I wrote it 😬) which makes it look like a custom thing, but it is not. It's just that it's difficult to find a consensus between those who want a superbuild and those who don't, and whatever we choose we will always get complaints 🙈.

The way it works is that our superbuild builds all the dependencies separately and installs them locally. And it points CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to that location. Then the MAVSDK project uses `find_package` for all of the dependencies, the standard CMake way.

If you look at [how we build MAVLink](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/third_party/mavlink/CMakeLists.txt), you'll see that we [install it locally](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/third_party/mavlink/CMakeLists.txt#L39-L44), like all the other dependencies. Then we [`find_package(MAVLink required)`](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/5379eed714f2fc18acd142b9613bb3890702b8dd/src/mavsdk/core/CMakeLists.txt#L4).

So you can totally point it to your own repo/hash (see [here](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/third_party/mavlink/CMakeLists.txt#L34-L35)):

```cmake
    ExternalProject_add(
        mavlink
        GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/mavlink/mavlink
        GIT_TAG ${MAVLINK_GIT_HASH}
        PREFIX mavlink
```

I am against `add_subdirectory` and `FetchContent`, for multiple reasons, including because it only works with dependencies that support CMake. I detail my opinion in more details [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/) if you are interested. Though I wrote this superbuild, I am now against superbuilds in general and I explain my reasoning [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-superbuild/), again if you are interested.

```
Well the dependencies are built by the superbuild, so it shouldn't be too hard to find them. Here they are: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/third_party/CMakeLists.txt.

> Well the dependencies are built by the superbuild, so it shouldn't be too hard to find them. Here they are: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/third_party/CMakeLists.txt.

I'm already submitting patches to upstream libraries. Please consider helping approve/merge the fixes, and working through a dockerfile in https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/issues/2665#issuecomment-3492948526.

From what I can tell, there is no place that MAVSDK actually checks out and builds TinyXML with superbuild disabled.
Instead, it builds the superbuild, then re-uses the built dependencies again with superbuild disabled, which isn't really a fair build.
All the patches that MAVSDK is doing to upstream libraries need to get applied too.

Saying that we need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect is currently a large hurdle due to the large amount of undocumented customizations, patches, and other oddities done. Would you consider an approach of a hybrid superbuild that allows some packages available through find_package, particularly `mavlink` to be included without burdening developers with compiling all dependencies manually for MAVSDK? I don't see the design choice to make superbuild binary for all dependencies.

> I'm already submitting patches to upstream libraries.

We've upstreamed quite a few patches over the years. Some of them were just not accepted. For instance TinyXML did not want to support older CMake versions at all. Now maybe our patch is obsolete (do we still support CMake 3.10.2? That was for Ubuntu 18.04 which is EOL, so I'm guessing we can just remove this patch 🤔.

> From what I can tell, there is no place that MAVSDK actually checks out and builds TinyXML with superbuild disabled.

Because that's the whole point of a superbuild, isn't it? Either the superbuild builds the dependencies, or you handle them yourself 😇.

> Instead, it builds the superbuild, then re-uses the built dependencies again with superbuild disabled, which isn't really a fair build.

I don't understand what you mean here. If you disable the superbuild, it doesn't build the dependencies, period. It will still run `find_package` for them, and it is your responsibility to provide them.

> All the patches that MAVSDK is doing to upstream libraries need to get applied too.

Only those that apply to your platform and are necessary for your build, but yeah. Again, if you don't use our helpers, it's your responsibility. Always better when patches are not needed, and I'm happy whenever we can remove one 😊.

> Saying that we need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect

You don't need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect. There are many other ways, e.g.:

1. You can fork the repo and modify the two lines you need to modify in the MAVLink helper in third_party. That's literally a 2 lines change.
2. You can run the MAVSDK configure step with superbuild enabled, have your own step that replaces the locally-installed MAVLink with your custom one, and then proceed with the build step.

> large hurdle due to the large amount of undocumented customizations, patches, and other oddities done.

I don't know if this is the goal, but this kind of value judgment (and it happened in other messages as well) sounds offensive to me. Remember that I am doing this for free, in my free time. And unless you're paying @julianoes, he's doing it for free as well.

> Would you consider an approach of a hybrid superbuild that allows some packages available through find_package

Most definitely not, it is out of the question for me. You are complaining that our build is "odd", and in the next sentence you ask that we made it even more complicated just for your specific use-case. Either you use the superbuild, or you deal with the dependencies manually. And "dealing with the dependencies manually" means that you can just copy-paste all our helpers and use that. If you want to do it differently (in docker, in a shell script, in a python script, with a package manager), you're free to do so.

> > I'm already submitting patches to upstream libraries.
> 
> We've upstreamed quite a few patches over the years. Some of them were just not accepted. For instance TinyXML did not want to support older CMake versions at all. Now maybe our patch is obsolete (do we still support CMake 3.10.2? That was for Ubuntu 18.04 which is EOL, so I'm guessing we can just remove this patch 🤔.

I believe this to be true. Both v9.0.0 and v11.0.0 of TinyXML have Config CMake support and require 3.15 to build.
At minimum. it appears safe to remove our `third_party/tinyxml2/cmake-3.10.2.patch`. The other `no-lfs64.patch` may still be needed, however I don't personally have the android experience to qualify that.

> > From what I can tell, there is no place that MAVSDK actually checks out and builds TinyXML with superbuild disabled.
> 
> Because that's the whole point of a superbuild, isn't it? Either the superbuild builds the dependencies, or you handle them yourself 😇.
> 
> > Instead, it builds the superbuild, then re-uses the built dependencies again with superbuild disabled, which isn't really a fair build.
> 
> I don't understand what you mean here. If you disable the superbuild, it doesn't build the dependencies, period. It will still run `find_package` for them, and it is your responsibility to provide them.

What I am getting at would that it would be helpful if there was a shell script, dockerfile, or CI file that built all the dependencies in a clean environment to show how to build without superbuild. I'm most of the way there (I think) from doing it in Docker. 

> > Saying that we need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect
> 
> You don't need to build with superbuild off to add a custom dialect. There are many other ways, e.g.:
> 
> 1. You can fork the repo and modify the two lines you need to modify in the MAVLink helper in third_party. That's literally a 2 lines change.

Fantastic, would you consider making the URL and hash CMake options so I can supply those arguments at configure time rather than needing a fork? If possible, I'd prefer to just keep up to date with upstream.

> 2. You can run the MAVSDK configure step with superbuild enabled, have your own step that replaces the locally-installed MAVLink with your custom one, and then proceed with the build step.


> > large hurdle due to the large amount of undocumented customizations, patches, and other oddities done.
> 
> I don't know if this is the goal, but this kind of value judgment (and it happened in other messages as well) sounds offensive to me. Remember that I am doing this for free, in my free time. And unless you're paying [@julianoes](https://github.com/julianoes), he's doing it for free as well.

To be clear, this is not a personal attack. I know it's hard to come off in messages that are having issues with the things you build/maintain, but I am 100% in support of helping improve MAVSDK, and keep both maintainers and users interacting in a sustainable way. I am well aware of the lack of funding, and unfortunately have never been in a position to fix that for the FOSS community. 

> > Would you consider an approach of a hybrid superbuild that allows some packages available through find_package
> 
> Most definitely not, it is out of the question for me. You are complaining that our build is "odd", and in the next sentence you ask that we made it even more complicated just for your specific use-case. Either you use the superbuild, or you deal with the dependencies manually. And "dealing with the dependencies manually" means that you can just copy-paste all our helpers and use that. If you want to do it differently (in docker, in a shell script, in a python script, with a package manager), you're free to do so.

Perhaps it would help if I demonstrate what that would look like? A lot of (small or big) projects do it, and I think it offers significant advantages for users in giving them the flexibility to rely on mavsdk to find dependencies they don't want to deal with but bring their own dependencies for the ones they want to change without requiring any source code changes to MAVSDK.

> At minimum. it appears safe to remove our third_party/tinyxml2/cmake-3.10.2.patch

It does indeed, thanks for the PR! 🚀 

> What I am getting at would that it would be helpful if there was a shell script, dockerfile, or CI file

From my point of view, it's all documented in code in https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/tree/main/third_party. I agree that the superbuild makes it harder to understand, but if you look at the individual CMakeLists for the dependencies, it's all really just like I describe in [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/).

Really, those contains exactly everything we need (including patches and compilation options) for the dependencies.

> would you consider making the URL and hash CMake options so I can supply those arguments at configure time rather than needing a fork? 

If you find a way to do it (I haven't looked into it), I say why not. My concern is that the superbuild scripts will make it convoluted. Again that is why I am now in favour of keeping the dependencies clearly separated from the project (again, [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/)) rather than having CMake build the dependencies as part of the project's configure step. This said, if we only provided helpers you would still have to somehow patch the MAVLink helper, so it would be similar to a fork/patch.

I would like to note that some of the "oddities" you find currently came exactly like this: "it makes it easier for the users if we do this automatically". So the happy path is just one command, but under the hood it adds complexity. That's why our CMake configure step requires python, for instance, because MAVLink needs it.

I am a bit of a purist here and came to think that we should simplify our build and delegate more to the users (making it their responsibility to understand how to build the dependencies, for instance). @julianoes is more pragmatic there, and I trust his judgement 😬.

> Perhaps it would help if I demonstrate what that would look like?

Why not, you would have to convince @julianoes here 😊. My way would be to remove the superbuild and just provide the helpers, and have users build like I describe [here](https://www.acarg.ch/posts/cmake-deps/). I know e.g. gRPC offers some kind of hybrid way and I personally find that it just adds complexity.
Sorry, I lost the thread here? What else needs doing?

answer_comments.body: May I ask which command you use to run multiple instances in gazebo?

It seems to me that MAVROS is the one binding to those ports:

```

        <arg name="ID" value="1"/>
        <arg name="fcu_url" default="udp://:14541@localhost:14581"/>

You can't bind both MAVROS and MAVSDK to the same port at the same time. So if you need both MAVROS and MAVSDK, you need to add new mavlink interfaces for MAVSDK.

comments.body:
For now, `mavsdk_server` does not support multiple drones (i.e. multiple drones running on the same MAVLink port, here 14540). Only MAVSDK-C++ does.

However, you can run multiple instances of `mavsdk_server`, each listenning to a different mavlink port, by using the latest `develop` branch of MAVSDK.

That would be something like:

```sh
./mavsdk_server -p 50040 udp://:14540
./mavsdk_server -p 50041 udp://:14541
./mavsdk_server -p 50042 udp://:14542
```

And then you could instantiate multiple instances of a wrapper. For instance in Python:

```python
from mavsdk import System

...

drone1 = System(mavsdk_server_address="localhost", port=50040)
await drone1.connect()
drone2 = System(mavsdk_server_address="localhost", port=50041)
await drone2.connect()
drone3 = System(mavsdk_server_address="localhost", port=50042)
await drone3.connect()

...
```

And then you could use your drone objects (`drone1`, `drone2` and `drone3` separately):

```
await drone1.action.arm()
await drone2.action.arm()
await drone3.action.arm()
```
Might be nice to add a FAQ on this in https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK-Python#mavsdk-python - since we get quite a lot of questions. Depends on how soon you think this will be done "properly".

title: mavsdk_server doesn't check if the server it is connected to is MavSDK.
author: AlexisTM
body:
## Problem:

If another gRPC server is already on port `50051`, MavSDK connect function succeeds, while the mavsdk_server starts and silently fails in the background.

For us it was `QIKService3`, some Qualcomm service for board discovery, which was listening on `tcp6://0.0.0.0:50051`.

Ideally, there should be a verification the server we connected to is valid.  

## To reproduce

Instal `QIKService3` or a gRPC test server on 50051.
I tried netcat listening on port 50051 without success, so I suppose  it probably needs to be a gRPC server.

```python
import asyncio
import logging
import sys
from mavsdk import System

logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.DEBUG)

drone = System()
await drone.connect(system_address="udp://10.151.60.12:14550")
# This succeeds even if no drone is connected because a server listen on 50051
version = await drone.info.get_version()
# This causes an error because get_version is not implemented.
# mavsdk_server dies silently in the background 
```

By default, the logging does not report those errors.

answer_comments.body:
> A system identification would do the trick, do a gRPC call which ensure we are connected to a mavsdk server?

Would it, though? If `mavsdk_server` starts successfully, then you will eventually receive MAVLink messages (that's your system identification). If `mavsdk_server` fails, you won't receive any MAVLink, but your gRPC "identification" call will fail just the same.

As you say, `mavsdk_server` knows that the port is already bound, and fails:

```
DEBUG:mavsdk.system:[01:07:14|Error] Failed to bind server to port 50051 (grpc_server.cpp:172)
DEBUG:mavsdk.system:Failed to start, exiting...
```

So to me, your problem here seems to be that somehow you did not have access to the `mavsdk_server` logs. Any kind of automation we would put on top of this would result in you getting the error message where you want it (because if the port you want to use for `mavsdk_server` is already bound, there is no way it will ever work).

Maybe my question would be: why did it take a long time for you to access the `mavsdk_server` logs, and do you think there is something that could make it easier? My feeling is that it is a bit of a leaky abstraction: users have to understand that there is a server running under the hood, so that if it doesn't work they immediately go check its logs :thinking:.

What do you think? :innocent:

> If connect() would check that mavsdk_server was successfully running and throw an exception otherwise instead of continuing as if everything is fine, that would solve the issue here I believe.

How would `connect()` make the difference between `UNIMPLEMENTED` and "mavsdk_server has stopped"? Or between "mavsdk_server has stopped" and "mavsdk_server did not start (e.g. the executable was not here)"?

> Yet another option would be to check the port before launching mavsdk_server and warn or throw an exception if it is not free.

Hmm it feels like a hack to me :sweat_smile:. But nothing prevents you from doing it from your code, before you start MAVSDK!

> Another option that would help is if we can promote mavsdk_server errors to loglevel error instead of debug.

Maybe there is something to do there, though I assume that users may end up turning the MAVSDK logs off (the issue here exists because at least you guys don't keep them enabled all the time, so it seems like a fair assumption :grin:).

Maybe there is something to do with the return code of `mavsdk_server`? Like MAVSDK-Python could detect that `mavsdk_server` stopped (with or without an error code) and... I don't know... throw an exception in Python? But then again, the exception would say "something wrong happened with `mavsdk_server`, please check the logs" :see_no_evil:.

I would be happy to see a good solution to that, but I guess my conclusion is that I don't see one myself :innocent:. Open to your suggestions of course!

> Yes, logging if the process exits before we expect it to would be a step in the right direction and most likely sufficient. Do you have any objections to this solution?

No, I think it would make sense for MAVSDK-Python to monitor `mavsdk_server` when it runs it :+1:.

My personal opinion is that by trying to always automate all use-cases, we make everything more complicated and we never address all use-cases.

I see MAVSDK-Python running mavsdk_server on 50051 by default as a "quick convenience" when we want to test something in the REPL. But for a production app, I would always have my application run mavsdk_server itself and connect MAVSDK-Python to it. That way my application can run mavsdk_server on an ephemeral port (possibly multiple instances of MAVSDK-Python).

author: junwoo091400

answer_comments.body:
Nice post! Two questions:

1. Shouldn't PX4 send `MAV_SYS_STATUS_SENSOR_GPS` when it is actually ready to fly with it? Or is it a misinterpretation by MAVSDK and `MAV_SYS_STATUS_SENSOR_GPS` only means that the autopilot has a GNSS sensor (and nothing about the fix)?
2. If PX4 is using `MAV_SYS_STATUS_SENSOR_GPS` correctly, what would be the MAVLink way to know that it's ready to fly? Should MAVSDK look at the GpsInfo?

> MAVSDK to actually get the global position validity flag from the Commander

Is there a MAVLink way to do that?

> to actually get the global position validity flag from the Commander

Yes we should, you're right! Which flag would that be? Is there one in SYS_STATUS?
I think we should start to use `is_armable` in MAVSDK everywhere. And we should switch to the events interface at some point. Contributions welcome :).

I'm not actually sure we should depend on the estimator status. That seems like a bit of an implementation detail that we should not depend on. Ultimately, the system status and events system is what we should rely on. I'm closing this. Please comment if anyone disagrees.

author: varunvp
body:
I want to write a DroneCore program to control a swarm of SITL PX4s simultaneously, through offboard mode. Right now, I'm using a swarm of 4 drones, which is a modification of the scripts here:https://dev.px4.io/en/simulation/multi-vehicle-simulation.html. I've been using the takeoff_land example program from DroneCore as a base, When I run the example program, the first drone with a sysid of 1 takes off, which is as expected. Now if I have to control all the 4 drones, I have to add the 4 UDP ports of the drones, which I did, as below.

```
DroneCore::ConnectionResult connection_result = dc.add_udp_connection(14540);
dc.add_udp_connection(14541);
dc.add_udp_connection(14542);
dc.add_udp_connection(14543);
```

Of all these, I just want to add device for one drone, for the sake of testing. 
` Device &device = dc.device(1/2/3/4(mavlink sys ids));`
Now here comes the problem. It seems that all the PX4 SITL drones have the same UUID, so even differentiating between the MAVLink sys id 's is useless, because DroneCore won't even consider them. So I had to comment out this part of code from device_impl.cpp, so that it forces use of sys id.

```

title: Landed State is jumping between modes
author: shrit

answer_comments.body:
The flight mode is sent with every `heartbeat`, usually at 1Hz. The landed state is sent with `extended_sys_state` at 1 Hz for the normal link on 14550 but at 5 Hz for the onboard link on 14540.

https://github.com/PX4/Firmware/blob/7f63ed8202a0f9d74181cdd8e40624565947cbc9/src/modules/mavlink/mavlink_main.cpp#L1665

comments.body: Same issue [here](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/issues/1917). Author was unable to reproduce and we got around it by just using mavlink passthrough call to request all params. It's not as eloquent because we just use a timeout to determine when we've "should" have received all params. For us it was on startup connection so the delay in receiving the params was not an issue.

title: Adding support for ArduPilot
author: JonasVautherin
body:
## Context

A while ago, @peterbarker worked on adding support for APM in the SDK ([here](https://github.com/peterbarker/DroneCore/tree/ardupilot)). More recently, @jinchengde (and others) started looking into that, again. The goal of this issue is to discuss the high-level requirements and architecture.

## Benefits for APM

The project is architectured in such a way that everything relies on a C++ MAVLink implementation. Making this implementation compatible with APM means that APM will also get the language bindings ([Python](https://github.com/dronecode/dronecodesdk-python), [Swift](https://github.com/dronecode/dronecodesdk-swift), [Java](https://github.com/dronecore/dronecore-java) and future ones like [Javascript](https://github.com/mrpollo/DronecodeSDK-JavaScript)).

The interface common to all our bindings is defined [here](https://github.com/Dronecode/DronecodeSDK-Proto/tree/master/protos) and is used to auto-generate language-specific APIs (e.g. using RxSwift in Swift, RxJava in Java, and asyncio in Python).

## SDK architecture (overview)

The SDK can been seen as composed from 4 parts:

1. The [interface definition](https://github.com/Dronecode/DronecodeSDK-Proto/tree/master/protos) (protobuf files), common to all the languages (C++, Swift, Java, Python). Each proto file is considered a "plugin", which is a group of (MAVLink) features.
2. The C++ [MAVLink implementation](https://github.com/Dronecode/DronecodeSDK), which actually maintains a connection to the drone and does the MAVLink logic.
3. The [backend](https://github.com/Dronecode/DronecodeSDK/tree/develop/backend), which exposes the C++ implementation of (2) as a messaging server through the interface of (1).
4. The language bindings ([Python](https://github.com/dronecode/dronecodesdk-python), [Swift](https://github.com/dronecode/dronecodesdk-swift), [Java](https://github.com/dronecore/dronecore-java)), which implement (1) to communicate with the backend (3).

At the lowest level, each plugin (defined by one proto file) is a C++ library. The backend uses those libraries, as can been seen [here](https://github.com/Dronecode/DronecodeSDK/blob/develop/backend/src/CMakeLists.txt#L38-L46).

I can see different ways to achieve that (and I'm looking for more thoughts). I believe that for each feature, there can be 3 situations:

1. The feature has (can have) the same interface between APM and PX4, but not the same MAVLink implementation
2. The feature does not have the same interface between APM and PX4, and therefore not the same MAVLink implementation
3. The feature is compatible between APM and PX4

Because features are grouped into plugins, that applies to plugins as well. The following scenarios could then occur:
1. We could keep the same interface (public headers) and build a different library that could be "swapped": for instance `libdronecode_sdk_apm_mission` and `libdronecode_sdk_px4_mission`, in case mission shares the interface but not the implementation. If the differences are really small, we could also imagine building the same library, but having an interface to decide whether it should start as PX4 or as APM (seems to me that it is what @peterbarker started [here](https://github.com/peterbarker/DroneCore/tree/ardupilot)).
2. In this case, we could possibly have a separate plugin definition (e.g. `mission_px4.proto` and `mission_apm.proto`), and therefore a separate implementation.
3. There is nothing to do here, it should just work

The questions I have would therefore be:
1. Do we have plugins that are completely compatible between APM and PX4 (e.g. [Action](https://github.com/Dronecode/DronecodeSDK-Proto/blob/master/protos/action/action.proto))?
2. What are the features that are not compatible?
3. For the features that are not compatible, could we share the higher-level interface (at the proto file level) and hide the difference as an implementation detail, or do we have to expose a different interface?

Great contributions would be to test the current SDK against an APM SITL and list the features/plugins that are working or not, and possibly why.

@auturgy and @peterbarker probably the best people for this. Generally speaking the systems use the same messages to achieve the same things, and will often use the same "main" message sequence. They may however use different sequences for edge cases, or use things that are not clearly defined in the spec.

The ones with highest impact are parameter protocol, mission protocol and command protocol. 
- Param protocol *high level* differences here: https://mavlink.io/en/services/parameter.html#implementations
- Mission protocol high level differences: https://mavlink.io/en/services/mission.html#implementations
- Command protocol differences are not documented yet (so I don't know what they are). The main difference is that I believe ArduPilot does not use the LONG form of commands, so suffers rounding errors for positional messages. 

In addition, ArduPilot uses different modes - ie Guided vs Offboard and may require different sending rates when in these modes. 

I expect you'll discover lots more. Let me know - then I can document them :-)

It seems that one aspect on which MAVSDK relies and where PX4 and APM differ is the flight modes. Flight modes are not part of the MAVLink specification, and MAVSDK currently uses the PX4 definitions (because it is developed and tested against PX4). However, there has been work towards specifying common flight modes (see e.g. [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LIcfOL3JrX-EznvXArna1h-sZ7va7LRTteIUzISuD8c/edit)).

The current state, as far as I can tell, is that the PX4 community is open to working on a flight modes specification and updating PX4 to comply with it, but this cannot be done unilaterally. Anybody wanting to work on that part on the ArduPilot side would be more than welcome to the discussion :blush:.

title: SIGABRT when destructing mavsdk
author: jperez-droneup
body:
In order to start fresh after detecting a disconnect (we want to reconnect on a potentially different IP address), we have to destruct the mavsdk object and create a brand new one. However, I have seen 2 exceptions come up when destructing the mavsdk.

I have attached a CMakeLists.txt and relevant minimal examples. Change the source `.txt` files to `.cpp`. Here is the CMake line:
`cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug ..`

It is also worth noting that I am connecting to the simulator using a remote port and UDP. Usage is similar to `mavsdk_server`:
`case1 udp://<url>:14540`. I am also using a REQUIRED code change from [this PR](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/2074) to allow the UDP disconnect to be properly recognized.

1. When registering on the `subscribe_is_connected` and then killing the simulator after a successful connection, I get a SIGABRT on [this line](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/ea0b720538cff8e51947557234cb9c4300edadc3/src/mavsdk/core/mavsdk_impl.cpp#L53). I made sure to unsubscribe from all subscriptions before destructing the mavsdk, but it still seems to be holding onto something. The error on screen is `libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::__1::system_error: thread::join failed: Resource deadlock avoided`. I have attached this as case1.cpp. This code gives you 120 seconds to kill the simulator and detect the failure.
2. After the mavsdk is destructed, it looks like the system_thread is still running, but the `_parent.time` has been uninitialized and leads to a `EXC_BAD_ACCESS (code=1, address=0x10)` exception on [this line](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/ea0b720538cff8e51947557234cb9c4300edadc3/src/mavsdk/core/mavsdk_time.cpp#L45).

[CMakeLists.txt](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/files/11702438/CMakeLists.txt)
[case2.txt](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/files/11702441/case2.txt)
[case1.txt](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/files/11702442/case1.txt)

Initial discussion conducted on [discord](https://discord.com/channels/1022170275984457759/1116075629008392314)

title: Handling of MAVLINK params
author: ykhedar
body:
I just stumbled upon the function which handles the MAV_PARAM types and found that the function in :

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/a6836be251e216f9967183a7551cc6ccb2a60382/src/mavsdk/core/mavlink_parameters.cpp#L923

handles it in a different way then the function for handling MAV_PARAM_EXT types. Is there a reason for this? Even the setting of `_value` in this function seems to be odd. Since the `temp.int32_value` is never assigned a value, using it to assign it to `_value` seems to give it garbage values. Or am I missing something?

answer_comments.body:
> @bazfp no, why? So you're saying we should use `std::variant` instead? I mean we should anyway but I don't understand why it's UB.

In the past I have looked at "correct" C++ type-punning alternatives and if i'm honest, I don't like them.

https://stackoverflow.com/a/11996970

As the saying goes, if it ain't broke...

> apm has in addition int8, int16 as well), the int8 and int16 param type was not being handled in the function tagged in my OP.

Aha, I understand! I was under the impression ArduPilot only has float and nothing else.

@ykhedar thanks a lot for your investigation. And sorry for not answering earlier, I've been very busy.

> 1. Addition of SetIntParamRaw() and modifying IntParam to include the param type to the param.proto file. This is done because the knowledge of the param type needs to be sent to the Param plugin to convert the int type to the float type.

So I see two ways here:
A) Add the type, as you suggest.
B) Always download all params on startup to then have the type cached when the function is used. This would take longer but make the API easier. What do you think?

> 2. In function: float MAVLinkParameters::ParamValue::get_4_float_bytes() const

That's crazy, I can almost not believe that this implementation is different, that's hilarious, and sad.

> The implementation uses the same message types and workflow. The main difference is that ArduPilot encodes data within parameter message value fields (floats) using a normal C cast rather than a byte-wise copy (and expects incoming messages to use the same encoding). I guess whatever is true, we need to handle it correctly on the MAVSDK side, so it matches. And then make sure to have a standard going forward that defines this properly.

Hi again, 

In the past few days I did some more research on the parameter handling related to PX4, Ardupilot and the current state in MAVSDK.

MAVLINK standard supports: uint8, int8, uint16, int16, uint32, int32, uint64, int64, real32, real64
PX4 supports/uses:                int32 and real32(float)
as found from [PX4 Param Reference](https://docs.px4.io/v1.9.0/en/advanced_config/parameter_reference.html)

Ardupilot supports/uses:         int8, int16, int32, real32(float)
as found from [APM Copter Param Reference](https://ardupilot.org/dev/docs/mavlink-get-set-params.html#setting-a-parameter)

MAVSDK supports int32 and float(real32)

Desired behavior for a Autopilot Param service:
1. getting a param
2. setting a param
3. getting all params

The desired behavior works for PX4 autopilot. Now to support the other data types in the param service, i have considered the following two options:

**Option A: Change the param.proto file to also support getting and setting of other data types.** 

This is not possible sadly since protobuf do not support int8, int16. Dont know if there is a workaround this.

**Option B: Making changes to mavlink_parameters.cpp.**

The following function: 
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/9b4b79cbdfca361fab9a528ba78e81376503cbd0/src/mavsdk/core/mavlink_parameters.cpp#L455

handles the parameters exchanged between the mavsdk and autopilot. 

In this function, the block of code in the if statement (which is to process the response of GetAllParams) works for ardupilot as well if I make the necessary changes in the function:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/9b4b79cbdfca361fab9a528ba78e81376503cbd0/src/mavsdk/core/mavlink_parameters.cpp#L915

The changes are mostly to add cases for missing data types (int8 and int16 for ardupilot).

The problem comes while GetParamInt/GetParamFloat since then the function to check the data type of the param is called:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/9b4b79cbdfca361fab9a528ba78e81376503cbd0/src/mavsdk/core/mavlink_parameters.cpp#L508

because the `ParamValue value` is set from the received param from the autopilot which has the correct type and the `work->param_value` is either `int or float` since this is done while creating the `WorkItem work` in:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/9b4b79cbdfca361fab9a528ba78e81376503cbd0/src/mavsdk/core/system_impl.cpp#L770

Do we really need to do this, could not we infer this directly from the incoming data type?
In that case we could have a single api for getting and setting param irrespective for the data type and this would also make it generic and support all data types listed in the mavlink specification.

Looking forward to getting feedback on this.

I just did a dirty hack to implement option B and the changes are in the following commit: 

https://github.com/ykhedar/MAVSDK/commit/12eb9a7358aa2e2d870231735939a7db0af7a9ba

(Also contains a new example to test the param read for ardupilot.)

With this I am able to read all params one by one using `GetInt` and also together using `GetAllParams`. The only catch is, I am currently simply converting the int types to int32 and then using the existing Param api (`GetInt`) to read the params.

Next I will check the setting of params.

Hi, i did some more work to make the param set for all ardupilot params work and the changes required are in the commit:
https://github.com/ykhedar/MAVSDK/commit/b598ab169e30c98c21772bce2beaf9cfdc95c115

Most significant changes are:
1. Addition of SetIntParamRaw() and modifying IntParam to include the param type to the param.proto file. This is done because the knowledge of the param type needs to be sent to the Param plugin to convert the int type to the float type.
2. In function:
`float MAVLinkParameters::ParamValue::get_4_float_bytes() const` 

Adding if condition for int8, int16 types and using direct conversion to float type instead of using the `reinterpret_cast` as used for the int32 type. I think this is the main difference between how the PX4 and APM implementation for parameters differ as specified in:

https://mavlink.io/en/services/parameter.html#ardupilot

The trouble with the `reinterpret_cast` based conversion is that at the end the value 0 is set in the APM autopilot. Not sure if this is due to some other reason but when change the conversion to `std::stof` then i get the correct param set behaviour,

My guess is that the function 
`float MAVLinkParameters::ParamValue::get_4_float_bytes() const` 
needs to be different for PX4 and APM. I am not sure how best to implement that.

Looking forward to getting feedback on this and making the changes more general/robust for an eventual pull request.

title: "MAVSDK" and "Arducopter SITL" incompatibility (and fly_qgc_mission.cpp and QGC incompatibility)

body:
Hi,

I'm the current maintainer of [Rosetta Drone 3](https://github.com/The1only/rosettadrone), a MAVLink implementation for DJI drones.
We are testing MAVSDK to send a QGC mission to [Arducopter SITL](https://firmware.ardupilot.org/Tools/MissionPlanner/sitl/) using `fly_qgc_mission.cpp`.
We identified at least two issues:

- ISSUE 1: `telemetry.health_all_ok()` is always `false`
- ISSUE 2: Arducopter doesn't start the mission but disarms.

Everything works fine sending the mission from QGC to Arducopter SITL instead of using `fly_qgc_mission.cpp`.

```
Output of fly_qgc_mission.cpp:

	Waiting to discover system...
	Discovered autopilot
	Waiting for system to be ready	<--- BUG 1: blocks on while (!telemetry.health_all_ok())
	(Waiting disabled by me, for testing)
	System ready
	Importing mission from mission plan: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/imatronix/server/test/p9-quillota.plan
	Found 10 mission items in the given QGC plan.
	Uploading mission...Mission uploaded.
	Arming...
	Armed.
	

Output of arducopter.exe:

	...
	AP: EKF3 IMU0 is using GPS
	AP: EKF3 IMU1 is using GPS
	AP: Terrain: clamping offset 435 to 15
	AP: Arming motors
	ARMED
	Mode AUTO
	AP: Mission: 1 Takeoff
	waypoint 1
	
	(little pause, probably a timeout)
	
	AP: Disarming motors	<--- BUG 2: Unexpected disarm. Why? There is no problem when sending the same mission from QGC
	AP: Mission: 1 Takeoff
	DISARMED
```

Are this incompatibilities intentional?
How do we make this world better?

IMO `fly_qgc_mission.cpp` is suposed to send QGC missions, so I would expect it to speak the same language as QGC (or rename it to `fly_qgc_mission_in_unintelligible_accent.cpp`).

comments.body:
Regarding the health fields: that was just some proxy that I came up with which tended to work ok with PX4. It's not properly done as it should. It should probably depend on the `health.is_armable` flag instead which is basically [MAV_SYS_STATUS_PREARM_CHECK](https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#MAV_SYS_STATUS_PREARM_CHECK).
It would probably be a good idea to remove the `health_is_all_ok` in MAVSDK v2 and recommend `is_armable` everywhere.

Now when it comes to missions that's a bit harder because various items get interpreted differently, and then the mission transfer is also different, ArduPilot putting home into item 0 and starting with item 1 for the mission while PX4 just starts at 0.

For your exact problem, I'm not sure what exactly it is, but let's try to debug it and fix it.

> Are this incompatibilities intentional?

No, just the way things were standardized appropriately or interpreted differently and have developed from there.

> How do we make this world better?

There is a two-weekly MAVLink dev call where we discuss what gets added to MAVLink and how PX4 and ArduPilot can slowly become more compatible. However, progress is hard, because often to become more compatible requires changes which would break backwards compatibility or additions of new mechanisms which require implementing or add complexity.

But anyway, let's debug what you're stuck on and go from there.

Any chance you can provide me code or steps how I can reproduce the issue?

Thanks @julianoes,

I got `fly_qgc_mission.cpp` working with Arducopter SIT.
I had to disable the `telemetry.health_all_ok()` and set `AUTO_OPTIONS` = 10 in Arducopter SITL.
More info [here](https://github.com/ArduPilot/ardupilot/issues/22966).

But this was just the initial test.
Where I really need help is in getting MAVSDK / `fly_qgc_mission.cpp` to work with Rosetta, which already works fine with QGC.
I will create an issue here: https://github.com/The1only/rosettadrone/issues/120

Hi @kripper, nice work with Rosettadrone! 
I think QGC mission from a file would not work as it is. This is because APM expects slightly different mission sequences. As a side not, APM expects first mission item as the home position and second mission item as takeoff. QGC does this conversion when uploading the mission to the autopilot but the example file you mentioned does not.

Please use the [MAVSDK integration tests](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/src/integration_tests/mission_raw_import_and_fly.cpp) as basis for mission upload to APM SITL. There are two separate tests in this file, one each for PX4 and APM.

See how mission upload, arm and takeoff are executed in a sequence to run the mission with APM in this function: [APM Mission Raw Integration test](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/d3115f547f8a7dee4b6c61dea1211ca80101d4b9/src/integration_tests/mission_raw_import_and_fly.cpp#L90)

Also see how the mission plan is created in [Create Mission Plan Raw for APM](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/d3115f547f8a7dee4b6c61dea1211ca80101d4b9/src/integration_tests/mission_raw_import_and_fly.cpp#L151)

Hope this helps :)

Best,
khedar

> It would probably be a good idea to remove the `health_is_all_ok` in MAVSDK v2 and recommend `is_armable` everywhere.

Yes. Having a universal `is_armable` check that each fight controller knows how to interpret depending on their features and sensors is a good idea.

BTW, when sending the first mission from QGC, we get an error saying that the aircraft is unable to arm even when it 1) sends the ACK to the arm/disarm command, 2) send the ACK to the set-flight-mode command and 3) informs that the flight mode is GUIDED in the next heartbeat.

I think I have seen this also once with arducopter SITL.

I believe QGC then disables the arming check and it works the second time...or we switch the fight mode to auto to get Rosetta actually starting the mission.

This only happens with QGC. With the C++ example, the mission starts flawlessly. Anyway, we should better fix this issue with QGC.

> Now when it comes to missions that's a bit harder because various items get interpreted differently, and then the mission transfer is also different, ArduPilot putting home into item 0 and starting with item 1 for the mission while PX4 just starts at 0.

I don't see a problem if the first item is a set-home-location or a take-off. 
All models can and should support both sequences.

> There is a two-weekly MAVLink dev call where we discuss what gets added to MAVLink and how PX4 and ArduPilot can slowly become more compatible. However, progress is hard, because often to become more compatible requires changes which would break backwards compatibility or additions of new mechanisms which require implementing or add complexity.

Good. On the long term, it pays off.

Congratulations. I admire your work on QGC.
Tomorrow I'll try to replay some logs with QGC.
I was looking for a debugging tool for Rosetta''s ground based "fight controller" (MissionManager) that uses virtual sticks to fly the missions.
I experienced an issue that didn't occur in the simulator, so the logs are crucial.

> BTW, when sending the first mission from QGC, we get an error saying that the aircraft is unable to arm even when it 1) sends the ACK to the arm/disarm command, 2) send the ACK to the set-flight-mode command and 3) informs that the flight mode is GUIDED in the next heartbeat.

I think I see something similar often with PX4 but I never quite tried to get to the bottom of it. Or at least it's a similar "try again and it works on the second try" sort of thing.

Yes, it's like a first time timeout. I believe I've also seen a message saying something like "arm check disabled".
I believe this is on the QGC side.

title: CMake local install RPATH missing
author: Ryanf55
body:
I tried consuming a locally installed version of MAVSDK in another package's install, and MAVSDK's CMake target fails to correctly export the shared library destination on an installed target.
I suspected this is an rpath issue, and spent 2 hours trying various recommendations, but have not found a solution.
Here is a conference talk from a CMake maintainer specifically about this use case with rpath:
https://youtu.be/m0DwB4OvDXk?si=3TaOFA6OdxY4z5F6&t=2452

I tried his recommendation on MAVSDK, and that did not fix the issue.

To reproduce, here's a Dockerfile:

```docker
FROM ubuntu:22.04

WORKDIR /ws

# https://mavsdk.mavlink.io/main/en/cpp/guide/build_linux.html

RUN --mount=target=/var/lib/apt/lists,type=cache,sharing=locked \
    --mount=target=/var/cache/apt,type=cache,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y install \
        build-essential \
        cmake \
        git \
        python3 \
        python3-pip

RUN git clone https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK.git
WORKDIR /ws/MAVSDK
RUN git submodule update --init --recursive

RUN cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -Bbuild -S.
RUN cmake --build build -j8
# Install is slightly different not using the install target, but it's the same idea.
RUN cmake --install build --prefix install


RUN --mount=target=/var/lib/apt/lists,type=cache,sharing=locked \
    --mount=target=/var/cache/apt,type=cache,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y install \
        pkg-config \
        astyle \
        bluez \
        bluez-tools \
        libbluetooth-dev

WORKDIR /ws
RUN git clone --recurse-submodules --branch cmake-install https://github.com/ryanf55/RemoteIDTransmitter.git
WORKDIR /ws/RemoteIDTransmitter
RUN CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/ws/MAVSDK/install cmake -B build
RUN cmake --build build
RUN cmake --install build --prefix install
RUN ./install/bin/rid-transmitter
```

Just run `docker build . --progress=plain` and you will eventually get 
```
 > [stage-0 17/17] RUN ./install/bin/rid-transmitter:
0.378 ./install/bin/rid-transmitter: error while loading shared libraries: libmavsdk.so.3: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```

The example here is when I tried using an installed executable that links to MAVSDK.
The linkage to MAVSDK is using the standard target_link_libraries approach:
https://github.com/Ryanf55/RemoteIDTransmitter/blob/cmake-install/CMakeLists.txt#L37


FYI @dakejahl

RUN --mount=target=/var/lib/apt/lists,type=cache,sharing=locked \
    --mount=target=/var/cache/apt,type=cache,sharing=locked \
