title: Timesync adjustment for incoming messages is not implemented?
author: chengguizi
body:
Hi,

Thanks for maintaining this SDK, looking very promising!

However I am inspecting its implementation for PX4 integration. I realise the incoming messages from telemetry is NOT adjusted based on time offset estimated, Example here

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/e7231dc8f390b96f4682e6810ac3d2fe554b5b8b/src/mavsdk/plugins/telemetry/telemetry_impl.cpp#L966

Cross reference to mavros, the correct behaviour should be something like this.

https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/c035b8ff1ffb042db235648371f5d7d2e531fae4/mavros/src/plugins/imu.cpp#L425

Is this a missing feature? Anyway to work around this by applying the offset ourselves? I see the timesync data seems not exposed in the API. Thanks!

Related:
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/issues/1033

comments.body:
To add on, seems the filtering of time offset estimate is also missing

https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/master/mavros/src/plugins/sys_time.cpp#L406

Thanks for the words and nice write up!

Timesync itself should be implemented, however, you need to enable it for a system using `enable_timesync()`. However, I wasn't aware that we should be applying the offset. So you're saying that the offset should be included in all messages with a time_usec field, or just the IMU one?

Regarding filtering: I guess that would make the time sync work smoother, right? I would gladly take a pull request that implements and tests that.

Hi @julianoes , thanks for the quick reply. Yes, from what I know working with PX4 systems and mavros, all incoming messages should have synchronisation offset applied.

Another example on local_position here https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/c035b8ff1ffb042db235648371f5d7d2e531fae4/mavros/src/plugins/local_position.cpp#L163

Namely, the offset application should be done on the recipient, not the sender.

And yes, I am currently fixing it to test with PX4 system, but I can tell it gonna be quite breaking change to the codebase, particularly if we want to fix all the incoming messages. What I am currently doing:
- expose the time offset from the system object, and apply the offset to the messages outside the Telemetry callback
- for sending out information, I have to change code and make sure they are sending the monotonic clock instead.

If I am to do a PR, which version i should be working on? v1.4.12? I see the API is quite different from the master and I am not sure why.

Btw, I would like to know if MAVSDK supports the operation to run MAVSDK app on two Ubuntu machines, and talk to each other in UDP? Aka, none of them are actual flight controllers / autopilot. Would like to have the timesync working there as well.

I think given this changes the API it's probably best to do it for MAVSDK v2, so in the `main` branch.

What would be the point of two MAVSDK instances? Would one be the autopilot_server and the other one the client, or how would this work?

@julianoes ok! Let me move to MAVSDK v2 on the main then.

Is the master branch consider stable? Or is there a stable release so far for MAVSDK v2? I need to test it on real PX4 systems, so can't take anything too unstable.

For two MAVSDK instances. The use case is following:
- We might want two robotic system to communicate with each other over a (wireless) serial link. MAVSDK has the flexibility of doing TCP, UDP and serial which is great!
- For such two systems, we may not always have autopilot. They can be embedded Linux system. Would be great to enjoy the infrastructure built by MAVSDK if all possible. For both data transmission, proper message packaging and timesync.
Also, I cant seem to find any information about MAVSDK v2. What is the purpose / benefits for the main version upgrade?

> What is the purpose / benefits for the main version upgrade?

I can answer this :). It's really just semantic versioning. We have changed the MAVSDK API, and therefore the next release should increase the major version to indicate that it will break the build.

> Is the master branch consider stable?

In terms of what it does with MAVLink, I would consider it "safe" (at least as safe as 1.4.x). In terms of API, it may still have small changes before v2 is released (since that's an opportunity to change the API :innocent:). So the biggest consequence is that if you work against `main`, maybe once in a while when you update, it will break your build and you will have to fix it (maybe a function name changed, a typo was fixed, something like that).

>     * For such two systems, we may not always have autopilot. They can be embedded Linux system. Would be great to enjoy the infrastructure built by MAVSDK if all possible. For both data transmission, proper message packaging and timesync.

fwiw, yes, this is possible. Based on a few examples that @JonasVautherin made a few years ago, I made something similar. I use a server and client to communicate between a groundstation and a drone that does not use PX4 (DJI). For the same reason, I wanted to profit from the strength of MAVSDK/mavlink.

The code was from a PR branch I believe. Maybe @JonasVautherin can dig it up?

> The code was from a PR branch I believe. Maybe @JonasVautherin can dig it up?

Hmm I'd say it's unlikely to still work, that was a while ago (I would guess 2019). But with the `action_server` and `telemetry_server` (which did not exist back then), I think it should not be too hard to make something that looks like an autopilot.

@JonasVautherin

title: Feature req: pkgconfig for building
author: vranki
body:
The "standard" way of including libraries in linux is pkgconfig mechanism. This tells what headers and libraries must be included in the compilation process. Almost any library in linux distros ship with pkgconfig metadata file. Pkgconfig can be used from any build system including cmake and qmake.

Mavsdk currently does not ship with pkgconfig and it's not obvious how to build correctly when using other than CMake as build system.

answer_comments.body:
@vranki just realized it is done [here](https://github.com/leethomason/tinyxml2/blob/master/CMakeLists.txt#L123-L129), which could serve as inspiration:

```cmake
## pkg-config

configure_file(cmake/tinyxml2.pc.in tinyxml2.pc.gen @ONLY)
file(GENERATE OUTPUT tinyxml2.pc INPUT "${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/tinyxml2.pc.gen")
install(
    FILES "${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/tinyxml2.pc"
    DESTINATION "${tinyxml2_INSTALL_PKGCONFIGDIR}"
    COMPONENT tinyxml2_development
)
```

Using the following `tinyxml2.pc.in`:

```pkgconfig
prefix=@CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX@
exec_prefix=${prefix}
libdir=${exec_prefix}/@CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR@
includedir=${prefix}/@CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR@

Name: TinyXML2
Description: simple, small, C++ XML parser
Version: @tinyxml2_VERSION@
Libs: -L${libdir} -l$<TARGET_FILE_BASE_NAME:tinyxml2::tinyxml2>
Cflags: -I${includedir}
```
I started looking into it [(draft PR here)](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/1889). Happy to get feedback :+1:
@vranki could you please give feedback on the draft PR by @JonasVautherin in https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/1889?

title: MAVSDK shows as "Vehicle 190"
author: petergerten
body:
My Setup:
```
PX4 SITL <-> Mavlink Router <-> MAVSDK
                            <-> QGC
```

When using the MAVLink Inspector in QGC, I can see:
Vehicle 1 -> all expected PX4 SITL messages
Vehicle 190 -> HEARTBEAT, TIMESYNC

Why is MAVSDK showing as "Vehicle 190"?

Also I saw that UUIDs are used now - is there a good overview somewhere on how system ID vs. UUID come into play?

answer_comments.body:
> "Vehicle" would show the system ID

It does. We just return [`MAV_COMP_ID_MISSIONPLANNER`](https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#MAV_COMP_ID_MISSIONPLANNER) as the system id, which is "190". So I would say that the peculiarity is on MAVSDK's side :sweat_smile:.

I guess a ground control station like QGC, should have a sysid that is just unique in the network, and use `MAV_COMP_ID_MISSIONPLANNER` as the component id. I'm not sure what QGC does for the component id, but I believe its sysid is hardcoded to 255...

comments.body: @JonasVautherin My confusion is mainly because I though "Vehicle" would show the system ID, not the component ID. If not, what is a "Vehicle" in MAVLink terms?

> "Vehicle" would show the system ID

@JonasVautherin I for one would prefer it greatly if we could expose both the system ID as well as the component ID in the Configuration, and furthermore make this available in the gRPC bindings. Also, QGC's sysid is not hardcoded - it's set to 255 by default, but this can be changed under Application Settings -> MAVLink. After fishing through some old PRs on the QGC repo, it looks like it hardcodes the MAV_COMP_ID_MISSIONPLANNER as its component ID.

title: Can the gRPC server be started before mavsdk-server discovers/connects to a system?
author: divyanshupundir
body:
In some cases, applications using mavsdk may start before the UAV system starts and is discovered by the mavsdk-server. In this case, clients intending to connect to the mavsdk-server will effectively have to block because the gRPC port will not be available.

Alternatively, if the gRPC server is up and the port is available, the clients won't have to block and the channels that are running in the background will automatically start receiving data once the UAV system is discovered.

The earlier versions of the mavsdk-server used to behave in the same manner which made client-side implementation quite easy.

answer_comments.body: Yeah it used to be that mavsdk would create a "dummy" system to receive subscriptions and whatnot, but that's not the case anymore. So your app has to wait until the drone is discovered before it can start the subscriptions. `mavsdk-server` is just reflecting that :innocent:

That won't work because the server implementation now needs to discover a drone. If you do that, your subscriptions won't ever have an effect because mavsdk won't save them for when a system is discovered.

Unfortunately I think that you have to deal with that on your side...

In my opinion, a very good next step for MAVSDK-Java would be to remove the dependency on gRPC and use direct bindings instead (i.e. JNI), so that it would be much more lightweight. But it also means that the API would get closer to the C++ API, which does not allow that at the moment.

And there you would see why this is problematic: MAVSDK-C++ supports discovering multiple drones, so if you subscribe to, say, the position updates before a drone is known, then MAVSDK cannot know if you were meaning to subscribe to the first or to the second drone that appears. That's why this is delegated to the user, because they know their use-case (and MAVSDK doesn't) :grin:.

title: Add MAVSDK to Vcpkg
author: edalm
body:
[Vcpkg](https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg) is a package manager for C++ with many interesting features. It is based on CMake, supports multiple architectures, provides update mechanisms and integrates with any user project using CMake as its build manager.

Are there plans to add MAVSDK to Vcpkg? It would provide great benefits to developers using MAVSDK in their projects.

answer_comments.body: That would be a very good idea. I would have to read more about how it all works though. If you can give me pointers or instructions how to proceed that would be helpful.
Sounds nice! Wouldn't we need to check that our dependencies are available on Vcpkg, too? I guess we won't add a superbuild there, will we?

> EDIT: Therefore, MAVSDK wouldn't be responsible for building third_party libraries, as Vcpkg would do it automatically. These dependencies could then be linked using CMake's find_package().

That's already how MAVSDK works (i.e. all the dependencies are found with `find_package`). By default, we have `-DSUPERBUILD=ON`, which builds the dependencies at configure time and then sets `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` accordingly. But if you build with `-DSUPERBUILD=OFF`, it will get all the dependencies from your system.

So the way there would be to try to build with `-DSUPERBUILD=OFF` and to see if all of our dependencies are available in Vcpkg already. You can find them [here](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/tree/develop/third_party), but note that some of them are used for `mavsdk_server` (a.k.a. "backend") exclusively, as can be seen [here](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/develop/third_party/CMakeLists.txt#L19-L25). Which means:

Dependencies for MAVSDK-C++:
* jsoncpp
* tinyxml2
* zlib
* curl

Dependencies for `mavsdk_server`:
* All the dependencies of MAVSDK-C++
* libressl (or openssl or boringssl)
* cares
* protobuf
* absl
* grpc

I would start with MAVSDK-C++ (i.e. `-DBUILD_BACKEND=OFF -DSUPERBUILD=OFF`). @edalm can you check if Vcpkg has `jsoncpp`, `tinyxml2`, `zlib` and `curl`?

Awesome! I think you should try to go for it, then :slightly_smiling_face:. I would personally try to use Vcpkg to build MAVSDK first (as opposed to writing the portfile to make a package out of MAVSDK):

1. Clone MAVSDK
2. Setup your Vcpkg to get the dependencies (`jsoncpp`, `tinyxml2`, `zlib`, `curl`)
3. Build MAVDSK with the toolchain, as per your instructions above (don't forget to disable the superbuild). So something like:

```cmake
cmake -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=C:/vcpkg/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake -DSUPERBUILD=OFF -Bbuild -S.
cmake --build build
```

If this builds, it means that MAVSDK was built using the dependencies from Vcpkg. Next step would then be to write the portfile to make a package out of MAVSDK, I guess.

Thank you for considering this suggestion.

**Vcpkg Overview**

Personally, I have been using Vcpkg for some time as an end user. I find it a very useful C++ package manager, which provides an easy mechanism to search, install and update libraries for any supported architecture. This is especially useful when developing on Windows, since libraries can be automatically downloaded, compiled and installed on a single directory, which can then be targeted with CMake rules.

In summary, Vcpkg downloads the library's source code from a public URL (e.g., GitHub repo), compiles the code for the chosen architecture, and installs the library on the predefined Vcpkg directory containing all installed libraries.

Then, developers who want to use these libraries in their projects only need to add Vcpkg's CMake toolchain by appending the following flag to CMake:
"-DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=C:/vcpkg/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake"

**Contribute MAVSDK to Vcpkg**

Vcpkg's GitHub page contains instructions on how to add a new library to Vcpkg.
* https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#new-package-guidelines
* https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/tree/master/docs

2. ```"portfile.cmake"``` with the rules on how to download, compile and install the library.

Optionally, patches may be provided in order to fix temporary issues either with Vcpkg or the project itself.

comments.body:
> `goto_location`

This sends a command (which is acked), so it's for one off / slow (max around 1 Hz) setpoints. For PX4 this uses the existing smoothing, etc. like in any auto/mission mode. For ArduPilot, I'm not too sure.

> `set_position_global`

This uses what is called OFFBOARD mode in PX4 and GUIDED in ArduPilot. You typically send this message at a rate faster than 2 Hz and continuously update/send it. For PX4, this does not do any smoothing but is more direct input.

> `set_actuator`

This is for one off commands to e.g. move a servo to do a specific action. It's not meant for smooth operation.

> `set_actuator_control`

This one is again using OFFBOARD/GUIDED mode and for smooth control. However, it is not supported by PX4 in later versions (I think since around 1.14). For ArduPilot, I'm not sure, you'd have to try it.

> And, calling ManualControl::start_position_control() in my ardupilot rover SITL, it print err:

title: Double Unlock in LockedQueue::Guard
author: grantwilk
body:
## Problem

- The `LockedQueue::Guard` class locks the mutex in constructor and unlocks in destructor
- `wait_and_pop_front()` manually unlocks the mutex, then re-locks with `unique_lock`
- When the method returns, both the `unique_lock` and `Guard` get destroyed as they leave scope
- The `unique_lock` destructor AND `Guard` destructor try to unlock the same mutex
- This causes undefined behavior (double-unlock) that can crash/hang the program

Personally I experienced this causing indefinite hangs in my application.

## History

- First observed in v3.7.0 release
- Does not reproduce in v3.6.0 release
- Likely introduced in commit https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/commit/1abe3ea074e3c340d6c26865788a5980826a1c8e by @julianoes

title: Add support for disabling native heartbeat sending and triggering HEARTBEAT over gRPC
author: tpayne-censystech
body:
I would like to contribute a feature that lets MAVSDK users disable internally generated HEARTBEAT sending and instead trigger transmission through gRPC.

The gRPC API would be a fail-closed, one-shot request to send a single MAVSDK-configured HEARTBEAT, not a toggle or persistent enable state. If the client stops calling, disconnects, or fails, MAVSDK does not continue sending heartbeats through that path. The client is responsible for calling at the desired rate (e.g. ~1 Hz).

The gRPC call would not set HEARTBEAT fields; MAVSDK continues to own message content (sysid, compid, mav_type, etc.). The call only requests that MAVSDK send its configured heartbeat.

Some integrations need an external process to control when MAVSDK sends heartbeats, while MAVSDK still constructs the actual MAVLink HEARTBEAT message. This avoids duplicating heartbeat construction outside MAVSDK.

**Proposed Solution**
- Add a configuration option (e.g. automatic_heartbeats_enabled) to disable native heartbeat sending.
- Add a gRPC API to trigger one configured HEARTBEAT per request.
- Optionally expose via mavsdk_server CLI (e.g. --no-automatic-heartbeats).

Default behavior stays unchanged.

Also you mention gRPC so I assume you are using some MAVSDK bindings. Which ones? MAVSDK-Python?

Yes, that is the main use case.

We are using MAVSDK to interface with a PX4 vehicle from our own application. We want the heartbeat to represent the health/presence of the application using MAVSDK, not just whether MAVSDK-server is still running.

If that application crashes, disconnects from MAVSDK-server, or stops servicing the control path, we want PX4 to see the GCS/companion component as offline so it can trigger the configured MAVLink lost-link failsafe behavior, such as RTL.

We also have test cases where we want to continue subscribing to telemetry from PX4 through MAVSDK, while intentionally disabling outbound heartbeat transmission so we can verify PX4's lost-link behavior.

We are not using MAVSDK-Python. We are using our own application that communicates with MAVSDK-server over gRPC.
I guess that would be acceptable as a feature. What do you think @JonasVautherin? Either explicit heartbeat triggering, or a timeout that stops it?
I like the timeout idea as long as it can be configured at runtime.
Yeah I think it should work 👍

Thanks @JonasVautherin 

Following the timeout idea @julianoes suggested, I’m planning to implement this as a heartbeat watchdog (deadman timer) rather than the original one-shot “send one HEARTBEAT per gRPC call” design.

The idea is that MAVSDK keeps sending periodic heartbeats as it does today and still owns the message content (sysid, compid, mav_type, etc.). The client’s job is to keep feeding the watchdog over gRPC at roughly the desired rate. If the client crashes, hangs, or disconnects and stops feeding, heartbeats stop after the configured timeout so PX4 can treat the GCS/companion as offline and trigger lost-link failsafes like RTL.

The timeout would be configurable at runtime, and default behavior would stay unchanged when the watchdog isn’t enabled. That should cover both our production use case (heartbeats reflect application liveness, not just mavsdk_server) and our lost-link testing (subscribe to telemetry, stop feeding, verify failsafe behavior).

Let me know if that direction works for you and I’ll open a PR.
Yes that works for me 👍

answer_comments.body:
The first command is supposedly the home position, or in this case it's just nothing, so not set as part of the mission.

What you need to do now is to parse the space separated values that you have above and map them to the mission_raw fields.

It looks like the format is described here:
https://mavlink.io/en/file_formats/#mission_plain_text_file

It would be nice to create an importer for this. Let's keep this issue open as a feature request.

Contributions are welcome :smiley:.

public fun uploadMission(waypoints : ArrayList<LatLng>, currentPos : Location)

title: Connection URL for DroneCore applications

body:
As DroneCore supports multiple connection interfaces TCP, UDP & Serial, we need to allow user to select either of them while launching the application.
Examples of connection URL could be:

- UDP: `udp://[bind_host][:port]`
- TCP client: `tcp://[server_host][:port]`
- Serial: `/path/to/serial/device[:baudrate]`

For.eg below conn URL _binds to UDP port 14500_
```
$ ./takeoff_land udp://:14500
```
binds to default UDP port 14540
```
$ ./takeoff_land
```
Connects to TCP Server (`192.168.8.2:5760`) hosted by MAVLink Router on Intel Aero
```
$ ./takeoff_land tcp://192.168.8.2:5760
```
etc.

For instance, let's say I have a sensor that sends telemetry. Should it have its own component ID in the system and use a `TelemetryServer`? A ground station (or SDK thing) should not have to worry if a telemetry message originates from a Pixhawk with internal sensor or an additional thing with another component ID. By looking at the MAVLink message you could distinguish it but I doubt we usually need to know.

Secundary Board Computer (SBC): SYSID: 230, COMPID: 2
A. SBC requests mission list: PX4 handles it properly
B. SBC sends STATUS_TEXT message: PX4 relays properly, QGC thinks there is a different vehicle

Our current code in Dronekit:

```
# settings
mavlinkID = 230
fcID = float_to_int(vehicle.parameters['MAV_SYS_ID'])

def sendMsg(txt=''):
    global mavlinkID, fcID
    vehicle._master.mav.srcSystem = fcID
    msg = vehicle.message_factory.statustext_encode(10,"DSPS: %s" % txt)
    vehicle.send_mavlink(msg)
    vehicle._master.mav.srcSystem = mavlinkID
    print "DSPS info: %s" % txt

```

I believe things *should* work as intended and we should work towards fixing everything that doesnt work. But i also think an SDK should give the freedom to whatever you like, such as defining exactly what SYSID/COMPID you want to use for a specific case.

>  A. SBC requests mission list: PX4 does not handle a request from the same SYSID correctly

Let's fix this.

Let me add some context. The problem is that the SDK has a concept of system, and it will have the same problem as QGC for a message which is from another system. This means that the message won't even end up in the plugins and can't be consumed. If we change that, everything around multiple vehicles falls apart.

Thanks for the reports above! Are they known issues for QGC and PX4, or should we open new ones?

> But i also think an SDK should give the freedom to whatever you like, such as defining exactly what SYSID/COMPID you want to use for a specific case.

That's probably a philosophical question, and at least a design choice. If I design a library for manipulating JSON documents, it will probably be limited to parsing and writing _valid_ JSON documents. One may want a way to generate invalid documents with my library, so that they can read them with a buggy parser. But I would consider it a perfectly valid choice to say that my library only supports valid documents.

Same applies here: I wouldn't want to add a way to e.g. insert typos into MAVLink messages because QGC has a bug an reads "amtitude" instead of "altitude". 

We need to think carefully about the implications of adding complexity into our API, and in this case it may be much better to actually fix the bugs than to support them :-).

EDIT: I hadn't refreshed and missed @julianoes answers above :sweat_smile:.

>The problem is that the SDK has a concept of system, and it will have the same problem as QGC for a message which is from another system. This means that the message won't even end up in the plugins and can't be consumed.

Could it not look at the component id, i think all systems are fine with a different component id.

I am not sure what the current status is of the systemid bug in px4, i will check
There is also the concept of the targetID, if set to 0 it should always be forwarded by routers and consumed by clients.

@JonasVautherin i think a better analogy is a TCPIP wrapper, and if you would allow changing the header of the packet. There is nothing wrong with the format, and if it is your intention to have any reply be sent to a different ID then why would that not be allowed. If it is needed programmers will find a way anyway and start hacking stuff. If you make it clear that it is normally not the way it should work i see no reason to limit then from doing so

Good points there, indeed. 

Again, I'm not saying that it is bad to add those features. I'm saying that it may require some work, and it may have an impact on the design. So if the need right now is a workaround, I'd rather fix the bugs.
Unfortunately we need it backwards compatible

SDK runs on Secondary Board Computer (SBC).

SBC -serial-  Pixhawk -serial/radio- GCS
SBC -4G- GCS
SBC -WIFI- GCS

As you see we have 3 methods of communicating to the GCS
Wiring diagrams are listed here: https://www.verticaltechnologies.com/info/tech-specs-wiring-and-electronics

Ok, and Pixhawk is forwarding everything using the `-f` flag?

I don't understand which messages exactly need to get changed. And what's used to forward traffic on SBC?
Without reading the story here, I assume discussion must also apply to new [STATUSTEXT_LONG](https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#STATUSTEXT_LONG).

title: Yaw/heading not accessible in MissionItem class
author: mwshafer
body:
It seems that `MissionItems` don't include a vehicle heading, which would be really helpful. This could be accomplished by adding the following methods to the `MissionItem` class:

- `yaw_to()` (double degrees from N): Rotate the vehicle to the specified angle after reaching position set by `set_position()`.
- `yaw_for()` (double seconds): Rotate the vehicle for the specified time after reaching position set by `set_position()` at rate specified by `set_yaw_rate()`.
- `set_yaw_rate()` (double rotation speed in deg/s): Set the target rotation rate for vehicle yawing. 
- `set_yaw_departure_ned` (double degrees from N): Set the heading for after mission item (transition to next mission item)

I am not sure the last method would be needed if the heading specified by `yaw_to()` could be maintainted between waypoints. If it could, the last item would be redundant. If multiple headings are desired at a given position, they could simply be stacked as a series of mission items with the same position, but differing values set by `yaw_to()`. 

I have a project wherein we need to be able to specify the vehicle heading because we have a directional antenna attached. I'd like to transition to Mavsdk, but need this heading control capacity.

title: Cross-Compile for RaspberryPi Error
author: domib97
body:
Im planning to use MAVSDK only for c++ on a Pi Zero in combination with ardupilot. I followed the instructions of: Cross compilation using dockcross and got some errors: 
[CMakeError.log](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/files/4710919/CMakeError.log)
[CMakeOutput.log](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/files/4710920/CMakeOutput.log)

Do I really need this not-so-lightweight sdk if i only plan to use c++ or will it be easier to use the 
c_library_v2 ?

answer_comments.body:
Would you mind pasting here the command line you use and which failed? Also would be nice if you could paste the actual error you got.

> in combination with ardupilot

MAVSDK is developed and tested against PX4 (trying to have as few PX4-specific logic as possible), so you may have issues running it against Ardupilot. We are of course open to contributions if you're willing to improve Ardupilot support! :wink: 

> Do I really need this not-so-lightweight sdk

Could you elaborate on what you mean by "not-so-lightweight"? MAVSDK-C++ is pretty lightweight to me, as it has very few dependencies. The language bindings (MAVSDK-Python, MAVSDK-Java, MAVSDK-Swift, ...) do rely on `mavsdk_server`, which is indeed a bit heavier because it depends on gRPC. But in your case you mention MAVSDK-C++, so I would be interested in knowing what is "not-so-lightweight" there :thinking:.

> will it be easier to use the c_library_v2

And wouldn't it be easier to start from scratch, not even relying on `c_library_v2`? I would advise you go for whatever is easier for you. In my case, I find MAVSDK-C++ lightweight, and it is much more efficient for me to use it than to rewrite the whole MAVLink logic from scratch.

FWIW @domib97 To provide some context the `c_library_v2` provides "primitives" for packing and unpacking messages into buffers for sending out over streams, for common messages and for the main dialects.

What it does not do is understand anything about the [microservices](http://mavlink.io/en/services/). These are the sequences of messages that define what it means for two systems to be connected, how to exchange mission data, how to get parameters from the underlying system, etc. 
You can write all that yourself, but it can be very hard to get right, and will probably end up being "as heavyweight" as mavsdk.

ArduPilot users tend to use Dronekit (Python) or Pymavlink (Python) for companion computer code (and more recently onboard LUA scripts). They use mavproxy for routing. Dronekit-Python in particular does much of what the SDK does, but of course is Python only. It is optimised for ArduPilot. The downside is that it is not properly supported by anyone, though it does have a reasonable community.

If you want to use the SDK then you will need to write some plugins if you use features where ArduPilot is not compliant with the MAVLink spec (there are a few, in parameter and mission handling), or where the spec does not properly cover any flight stack (e.g. to get the ArduPilot specific modes). You will probably want to make sure that you can connect to their simulator. 
All that is a bit of effort, but if you want to use C++ probably actually a lot less then trying to write your own API. 

I recommend you go talk to ArduPilot on the ArduPilot/pymavlink gitter channel to confirm this advice. FWIW I would love to see ArduPilot support, heading towards convergence to the specification for all flight stacks.

The mavsdk_server is now built statically and provided by PyPi. We have no more need to do cross compilation, or building on a Raspberry Pi. If you still require it and run into problems, please create a new issue @domib97, thanks.

> in combination with ardupilot

MAVSDK is developed and tested against PX4 (trying to have as few PX4-specific logic as possible), so you may have issues running it against Ardupilot. We are of course open to contributions if you're willing to improve Ardupilot support! :wink: 

> Do I really need this not-so-lightweight sdk

Could you elaborate on what you mean by "not-so-lightweight"? MAVSDK-C++ is pretty lightweight to me, as it has very few dependencies. The language bindings (MAVSDK-Python, MAVSDK-Java, MAVSDK-Swift, ...) do rely on `mavsdk_server`, which is indeed a bit heavier because it depends on gRPC. But in your case you mention MAVSDK-C++, so I would be interested in knowing what is "not-so-lightweight" there :thinking:.

> will it be easier to use the c_library_v2

And wouldn't it be easier to start from scratch, not even relying on `c_library_v2`? I would advise you go for whatever is easier for you. In my case, I find MAVSDK-C++ lightweight, and it is much more efficient for me to use it than to rewrite the whole MAVLink logic from scratch.

FWIW @domib97 To provide some context the `c_library_v2` provides "primitives" for packing and unpacking messages into buffers for sending out over streams, for common messages and for the main dialects.

What it does not do is understand anything about the [microservices](http://mavlink.io/en/services/). These are the sequences of messages that define what it means for two systems to be connected, how to exchange mission data, how to get parameters from the underlying system, etc. 
You can write all that yourself, but it can be very hard to get right, and will probably end up being "as heavyweight" as mavsdk.

ArduPilot users tend to use Dronekit (Python) or Pymavlink (Python) for companion computer code (and more recently onboard LUA scripts). They use mavproxy for routing. Dronekit-Python in particular does much of what the SDK does, but of course is Python only. It is optimised for ArduPilot. The downside is that it is not properly supported by anyone, though it does have a reasonable community.

If you want to use the SDK then you will need to write some plugins if you use features where ArduPilot is not compliant with the MAVLink spec (there are a few, in parameter and mission handling), or where the spec does not properly cover any flight stack (e.g. to get the ArduPilot specific modes). You will probably want to make sure that you can connect to their simulator. 
All that is a bit of effort, but if you want to use C++ probably actually a lot less then trying to write your own API. 

I recommend you go talk to ArduPilot on the ArduPilot/pymavlink gitter channel to confirm this advice. FWIW I would love to see ArduPilot support, heading towards convergence to the specification for all flight stacks.

The mavsdk_server is now built statically and provided by PyPi. We have no more need to do cross compilation, or building on a Raspberry Pi. If you still require it and run into problems, please create a new issue @domib97, thanks.

title: Health not clearing cache
author: douglaswsilva
body: Telemetry Health Subscription does not clear cache when aircraft is disconnected, so if you turn aircraft off and on again, it will say it has home position and global position even though it has not locked GPS yet. This will prevent vehicle form taking off.

answer_comments.body:
@JonasVautherin 

1. I was wrong - removing the caching is still compliant. I have fixed up the wording in https://github.com/mavlink/mavlink-devguide/pull/204 to make this more obvious. 
2. I do not think we should cache parameters, but I do think we should make it possible for a user to build such a cache if they want, noting it will have the limitations of the underlying protocol.


The point of _any_ cache is to have a local copy that you can access quickly (and in the MAVLink case, to also reduce traffic on the link by not having to reload data). If you choose to use a cache then  either you have mechanisms to guarantee the cache is up to date, or you accept that it is OK for it to not be up to date. Otherwise you don't cache.

For parameters we could cache them because there isn't AFAIK "much cost of getting it wrong" (they very rarely change, and even if they do that mostly only matters if you're rendering a UI dependent on their values). On the other hand, most MAVSDK use cases don't rely on us needing to read parameters, or at least very many, and they don't rely on that process being very timely. So on balance, easier just not to cache.

For other values I do think caching makes sense, but we do need to think about this some more. I don't care if my battery level info is a few seconds old, but I may care if it is 10 minutes old. For altitude, I do care if it is more than a few seconds old. Upshot, maybe a cache needs to invalidate, or at least include a timestamp for some values.
Ok, I merged #847. Still the cache issue related to health is not solved, so I keep this issue open.
Note to self. Instead of using params for health checks we should switch to checking the flags of https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#SYS_STATUS.
Most health flags are now based on SYS_STATUS, so I'm closing this. They would also automatically be updated given SYS_STATUS is received at 1 Hz, usually.

Examples:

* Caching a "battery status" is fine, so that users receive the last position as soon as they subscribe to it instead of waiting until the next battery state (which may be a few seconds away).
* Caching parameters is fine if the autopilot broadcasts the new values whenever they change. It is not fine if MAVSDK has no way to know that the parameter was changed, and therefore we should just always request the param, with the caveat that sometimes this may time out.

title: Rename Telemetry APIs that does status update
author: shakthi-prashanth-m
body_code_blocks:
void request_flight_mode_updates(flight_mode_callback_t callback);
void remove_flight_mode_updates();

void unsubscribe_flight_mode_updates();

answer_comments.body:
> s I know, we have to call again same API by passing nullptr for the callback parameter 

OK, I didn't know that and it isn't documented. I don't think it matters so much what APIs we use for turning off callbacks as long as we are consistent across the whole of the core library and document this as a "standard".

Personally I actually prefer our current naming over your suggestion:
```
device.telemetry().flight_mode_async(callback); //enable callbacks
device.telemetry().flight_mode_async(nullptr); //disable callbacks
```
OR
```
device.telemetry().flight_mode_async(callback); //enable callbacks
device.telemetry().cancel_flight_mode_async(); //disable callbacks
```
I just think they feel "less wordy", and I don't think people find them confusing provided that we are consistent. 

I would go with the majority.

I would keep what we have now or go with @shakthi-prashanth-m's suggestion. Both are fine with me, I think `subscribe_` and `unsubscribe_` are action clearer (and also what we currently use in the manually derived wrappers. However, I'm not sure if it is worth changing it all right now since there will be some churn due to gRPC anyway.

title: udp://127.0.0.1 won't connect.  udp:// will.
author: linuxguy123
body:
To reproduce:

Take AutoPilot Server example, version 1.3.4.  Strip out all the code in main() except 

````while (true) {
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::seconds(1));
````
This creates a stand alone MAVLink server.   Edit Run it.

Run Takeoff and Land example.  

This IP address will fail, whether passed in on the command line or hard coded in add_any_connection().
```` 
./a.out udp://127.0.0.1:14551
````
This IP address will connect:
```` 
./a.out udp://:14551
````
MissionPlanner connects properly with 127.0.0.1 and Port 14551.

comments.body:
That's by design. When you add `127.0.0.1` you start sending UDP packets to that IP, rather than listening on that port. It's basically the same as the call https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/425577aa5629d591a854a65fd1f2dd6d88b526d9/src/mavsdk/core/include/mavsdk/mavsdk.h#L133.

Also check these docs:
https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/425577aa5629d591a854a65fd1f2dd6d88b526d9/src/mavsdk/core/include/mavsdk/mavsdk.h#L83-L86

Thanks for the prompt reply. 

Is this a general UDP thing or specific to MAVSDK ?

````
 For UDP, the host can be set to either: 
      *   - zero IP: 0.0.0.0 -> behave like a server and listen for heartbeats. 
      *   - some IP: 192.168.1.12 -> behave like a client, initiate connection 
      *     and start sending heartbeats. 
 ````

If this is the case, the IP addresses in the AutoPilot Server example are incorrect.   The APServer "server" portion, ie the AP, is set up with IP 127.0.0.1:14551.  The APServer "client" portion, ie the GCS is set up with upd://:14551.   According to the above, it should be the other way around. 

And why does MissionPlanner need an IP address to connect to the server ?  It works with udp:127.0.0.1:14551.

I saw that both the server and client used add_any_connection().   I thought the client/server functionality selection would have occurred when one set the configuration ie:

````
mavsdk::Mavsdk::Configuration configuration(
            mavsdk::Mavsdk::Configuration::UsageType::Autopilot);
        mavsdkTester.set_configuration(configuration);
````

or

````
mavsdk::Mavsdk::Configuration configuration(
        mavsdk::Mavsdk::Configuration::UsageType::GroundStation);
    mavsdk.set_configuration(configuration);
````

The CLI argument format is not a general thing, no. It's a format we adopted for MAVSDK. MissionPlanner uses it differently.

In my mind specifying `127.0.0.1:14551` to mean to listen on 127.0.0.1 doesn't actually make much sense. You're basically saying I want to listen locally but you can only listen locally, you can't listen "on another IP". All you can do is to listen on one network interface only, e.g. on your own IP 192.168.x.y, or for all 0.0.0.0 which is the same as not specifying it for MAVSDK.

---

> The APServer "server" portion, ie the AP, is set up with IP 127.0.0.1:14551. The APServer "client" portion, ie the GCS is set up with upd://:14551. According to the above, it should be the other way around.

I don't know APServer and how it works. One thing I know is that we seem to have it backwards in the PX4 (and probably ArduPilot) world. So if you consider the autopilot to be "the server", that's wrong, because generally the autopilot is sending out UDP packets containing heartbeats in broadcast and anyone can listen to them (locally) and then send UDP back.

In the web on the other hand a webserver is not sending out it's website on broadcast for anyone to listen but it's listening on its local port 80 for anyone wanting to get the website.

>  I thought the client/server functionality selection would have occurred when one set the configuration ie:

This mainly sets the component IDs.

title: Use 2 UDP ports for sending and receiving data

body:
Hello,

I am wondering if it is possible to setup mavsdk with a UDP connection where messages are received on one localhost::udp tuple and sent to another localhost::udp tuple.

Quick explainer: the method we used to go with in OpenHD has always been: 
On the ground unit,
1) listen for messages from the Ground controll application on one udp localhost port
2) send messages to the ground controll application on another udp localhost port.

So for example, the ground controll application listens on localhost::16550 and sends data to localhost::16551

However, I cannot see a way to configure mavsdk to listen and send to different udp ports.
Since the send udp port is automatically added by using the address and port of a received packet.

Best regards, 
Constantin

Say you run SITL on your computer. SITL sends UDP to localhost:14540 from some ephemeral port. MAVSDK listens on 14540, and therefore receives the messages coming from SITL. When it does, then it takes the ephemeral port it sees in those messages, and uses it to send messages back to SITL.

About asyncio, I was actually thinking about using RxPython. First of all because I love the reactive extensions, and because we already use RxSwift and we will quite definitely use RxJava. And I would prefer to keep the bindings consistent between the different languages. Do you know RxPython? What would be the advantage of asyncio over it?

Hi there,

Unfortunately I can't help on the C++ side, haven't had time to dig into C++11 yet.

As it comes to asyncio ad RxPython - I have used RxPython before, it is nice working with it but I am one of them who thinks callbacks are not really pythonic and do not improve code readability. Also I find it somewhat more easy to work with coroutines in asyncio! I also like the in-language keywords which make the general workflow much easier and faster.

Just a quick example:
```python
import asyncio
...
loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
...
async def test_coroutine():
    while True:
        # Blocks this coroutine and hands over to other coroutines,
        # until data becomes available
        battery_voltage = await get_battery_voltage()
        print(f"Battery voltage:{battery_voltage}")
        # This coroutine does want to sleep for 5 seconds
        # so the eventloop switches over to another coroutine
        await asyncio.sleep(5)

# Just an example function
async def get_battery_voltage():
    # Instead of creating a request and setting a callback
    # await blocks this coroutine until data is received
    # therefore code flow is not interrupted
    await system_0.get_battery_voltage()
    # Now do something with the received data, this would
    # be a callback function with RxPython

loop.create_task(test_coroutine()) # Keeps running
loop.run_forever() # Start the eventloop and run forever

```

Of course it would be better to use RxPython if we need to support Python 2.x and Python 3.4, `asyncio` is available since Python 3.5 and will receive a feature increase in the upcoming 3.7 release. A small bonus for asyncio - though not relevant as it is an additional dependency - is uvloop. When using uvloop it is possible to achive almost Go-like performence for networking tasks (could potentially be useful in applications that use DroneCore)

FWIW It will probably make things easier for documentation if all the front ends use similar paradigms (i.e. RxPython), but as a rule it is better to make it easier for end users. I don't know what is more familiar to Python developers - I haven't had any experience of either framework

Thanks for the example and for your contribution, @xvzf :-)!

> It will probably make things easier for documentation if all the front ends use similar paradigms

Documentation, development, maintenance and support. If all projects end up using the reactive extensions together with gRPC, they will essentially do the exact same thing, but in different languages. So most of what we learn from one project will apply to the others. People used to the swift SDK will be able to understand code written with the python/java SDK. If we do a completely different interface, they become different projects, and probably different maintainers.

> asyncio is available since Python 3.5

I don't have experience about Python 2 vs Python 3... How limiting is that? Can we assume every new project is running Python 3.5?

> I am one of them who thinks callbacks are not really pythonic and do not improve code readability.

How do you deal with an infinite stream without callbacks? Your example seems to be polling the battery every 5 seconds. But taking the telemetry, for instance, that's not how it works in mavlink, and that's not how it is implemented in our gRPC implementation. So my question is the following: would it imply that the python frontend would need to save all the values it receives, and wait for the client to poll for them?

The way it is implemented right now is using gRPC streams, so essentially callbacks. And that's why I feel like RxPy fits naturally there: it is a library for dealing with streams. Translating our streams to something that can be polled by asyncio seems like it is more complex and therefore prone to error. And not consistent with the other projects, which makes it more difficult to maintain.

What is your opinion on that, @xvzf? Since you've been using both RxPy and asyncio, I am very interested in your opinion :-).

> I don't have experience about Python 2 vs Python 3... How limiting is that? Can we assume every new project is running Python 3.5?

IMO being restricted to Python 3 is not the problem it was 3 or 4 years. Most really useful 3rd party libraries support both Python 2 and 3, and some big projects are moving exclusively to Python 3 - e.g. Django. 

I personally would prefer we support both, but would not put it as a requirement on the project.

> I don't have experience about Python 2 vs Python 3... How limiting is that? Can we assume every new project is running Python 3.5?

At work we switched to Python 3 two years ago, Python 2.7 will get updates, but not new features and is (related to the syntax) sort of incompatible with Python 3. Ubuntu 16.04 was already using python 3.5, the latest release is using 3.6.

> would it imply that the python frontend would need to save all the values it receives, and wait for the client to poll for them?

Sort of - I was thinking about a direct call and a non blocking socket, but when we are handling with streams and therefore this would not work

> What is your opinion on that, @xvzf? Since you've been using both RxPy and asyncio, I am very interested in your opinion :-).

We should go with RxPy, the gRPC client for python does not support asyncio  (https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/6046) therefore we'd have to develope some workarounds just for getting asyncio working with gRPC.
A "shared" framework would also be beneficial!

> We should go with RxPy, the gRPC client for python does not support asyncio (grpc/grpc#6046) therefore we'd have to develope some workarounds just for getting asyncio working with gRPC.

title: Its time to switch Coding style to Clang format
author: shakthi-prashanth-m
body:
Clang format is most popular C++ coding style: http://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormat.html
Benefits:
- We can also integrate this in git using [git-clang-format](https://github.com/llvm-mirror/clang/blob/master/tools/clang-format/git-clang-format) or add git pre commit hook.
- Clang has a [static analyzer](https://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/).
- It will rearrange header file inclusion order alphabetically (@JonasVautherin was this earlier).
- Supports various styles.
  - LLVM A style complying with the LLVM coding standards
  - Google A style complying with Google’s C++ style guide
  - Chromium A style complying with Chromium’s style guide
  - Mozilla A style complying with Mozilla’s style guide
  - WebKit A style complying with WebKit’s style guide

Reference:
http://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormat.html
http://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormatStyleOptions.html
https://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/
https://clangformat.com/ - Interactive guide and builder.

@julianoes @JonasVautherin @hamishwillee .

answer_comments.body:
I added a script to run clang-format to the [avoidance](https://github.com/PX4/avoidance/blob/master/tools/fix_style.sh) module last year. Maybe the script can help:

```
#!/bin/bash

STYLE="google"

if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <src_file | dir>"
    echo ""
    echo "ERROR: At least one source file or one directory must be provided!"

    exit 1
fi

for arg in "$@"
do
    if [ -f $arg ]; then
        clang-format -i -style=${STYLE} $arg
    elif [ -d $arg ]; then
        find $arg -iname *.h -o -iname *.cpp | xargs clang-format -i -style=${STYLE}
    fi
done
```

One thing, though, is that we probably don't want to refactor the whole project (regarding git history). I guess we would need to keep our current style unchanged, if possible. What do you think?

title: Mavsdk instances should not share mavlink_status_t
author: julianoes
body:
It turns out that `Mavsdk` instances will share `mavlink_status_t` if they are in the same compilation unit. This happens for instance when two `Mavsdk` instances are created in an integration test to talk to each other. In this case, they will access the same `mavlink_status_t` which is allocated `static`, so they will share the `seq` field.

The `static` status comes from here:
https://github.com/mavlink/c_library_v2/blob/636fae5ca34eff6007344718755d78fcdf94238e/mavlink_helpers.h#L29

The solutions I see are:
1. Use `_pack_chan()` everywhere, instead of `_pack()`. This would require all plugin code to be changed and also would require the Mavsdk instance to detect other Mavsdk instances using some sort of global data structure. Both things I would like to avoid.
2. Try to allocate the status in `Mavsdk` and use the `MAVLINK_EXTERNAL_RX_STATUS` define: https://github.com/mavlink/c_library_v2/blob/636fae5ca34eff6007344718755d78fcdf94238e/mavlink_helpers.h#L25 I'm not entirely sure how the mapping would work though.
3. Check the MAVLink C++ library to see if it handles it differently.

This can be observed in the Ftp integration test, e.g.

```

title: DroneCore shell, a command line tool for interacting with a MAVLink device
author: shakthi-prashanth-m
body:
This is about proposal of **DroneCore shell**, a command line tool for interacting with a MAVLink device using DroneCore library. Its will be a handy tool for both users & developers.
May be this was discussed sometime back in the community. I am just recording it here for tracking later.

I feel that its very suitable, if someone wants to try DroneCore quickly like,
```
$ dronecore action { arm | disarm | takeoff | land} [args]
```
```
$ dronecore mission { upload | download | set | } [args]
```
etc.

I imagine that such tools are going to become familiar with many users in future, as we see such powerful tools like **curl**/**wget** in URL transfer domain. I think with similar thought _mavros_ command line (`mavcmd`) was introduced ( I think so).

After python bindings in place, we may think of developing such tools relatively easily.
I shared this with @julianoes earlier. I just wanted to hear what is the feedback in the community.

Please share your thoughts.
Thanks.
body_code_blocks: $ dronecore action { arm | disarm | takeoff | land} [args]
$ dronecore mission { upload | download | set | } [args]

answer_comments.body: While this could be handy, I would vote to support easy scripting like this just in the Python library. The benefit that Python gives us is that you can inspect functionality using `help()` and it handles all command line parsing for you, etc.

I believe that the python bindings will naturally enable easy scripting, and making a DroneCore shell package would be a separate (subproject) of DroneCore.

I'll close it for now, as I believe that will come back with the python bindings (but on the python repo, then :)).
I think that makes sense. We don't need to re-invent scripting.

So it's not necessarily the UTC time but can also be time since system boot.

title: Support multiple callback-subscribers
author: potaito
body:
MAVSDK allows to subscribe to new information with callbacks, like for example updates to the Position telemetry:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/7244ace0d7b223e8e7618d8736769f4f2a2ef1f3/src/plugins/telemetry/include/plugins/telemetry/telemetry.h#L990-L993

In the implementation only one callback function is registered, and subscribing a second time would simply remove the previous subscription silently:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/7244ace0d7b223e8e7618d8736769f4f2a2ef1f3/src/plugins/telemetry/telemetry_impl.cpp#L2075-L2079

A `long` would already be better, yes :smile:. Weekend literature...

I started with a simple prototype for a registry: https://godbolt.org/z/hxhxsWc7M

Couple of points that are open:
1. Probably needs to be thread-safe, or have locks around it.
2. Should the callback itself be stored in a shared_ptr and then returned in the handle, so that if you destruct the handle, the callback is also destructed, and a weak_ptr in the registry can be checked and removed? It would be overhead but probably safer.
3. Should be one registry per mavsdk instance, or system, or per plugin, or per function?
4. Should it be a map instead of a vector? This probably depends on 3..

1. I would definitely vote for thread-safe, otherwise we will always lock around it
2. I don't think that's necessary, I don't see why a user would want to destroy a handle :thinking: 
3. I'd say per system. Definitely not in `Mavsdk`, as `System` should be as independent from it as possible. Per plugin/function sound like they will have their own edge cases (what if 2 functions from 2 different plugins want to subscribe to the same Event?)
4. What about a `Map<Event, vector<Entry>>`? What's called often is the `call(Event event)` function, and it applies only to the list of callbacks that are interested in that event.
FYI: this is coming soon in version 2: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/1768.

title: Set rate position and attitude_euler not working with ArduPilot
author: julianoes

linked_prs.title: telemetry: Use REQUEST_DATA_STREAM for ArduPilot set_rate

comments.body:
Hello @julianoes ,
Is this issue open for contribution? I am a first-time contributor and would be happy to work on it if you could assign it to me.
@lakhmanisahil sure go ahead and make a pull request if you have a solution for it. I'm not working on it at the moment.
Thanks, @julianoes . I am looking into this issue and will aim to submit a PR.

Hi @julianoes, I've been studying the source (no hardware yet) and I think the fix should go inside `telemetry_impl.cpp`. All the `set_rate_xxx` functions call `_system_impl->set_msg_rate()` / `set_msg_rate_async()`, which internally send `MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL` (cmd 511) — ArduPilot doesn't ACK this reliably on serial links. 

I can see `_system_impl->effective_autopilot()` is already used in `process_sys_status()`, so the fix would be to check `effective_autopilot() == Autopilot::ArduPilot` and fall back to `REQUEST_DATA_STREAM` instead for the affected rate setters. 

Planning to open a PR regarding this. Does that approach look right to you?

Files I'd change: [`telemetry_impl.cpp`](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/cpp/src/mavsdk/plugins/telemetry/telemetry_impl.cpp) · [`telemetry_impl.h`](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/main/cpp/src/mavsdk/plugins/telemetry/telemetry_impl.h)

Investigated the ArduPilot source — `MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL` is fully supported for both `ATTITUDE` and `GLOBAL_POSITION_INT`. The command is correctly handled, ACKed, and applied.

The actual root cause is **GCS stream rate override**: when another GCS application (MAVProxy, QGC, Mission Planner) on the same MAVLink link sends `REQUEST_DATA_STREAM`, ArduPilot's `initialise_message_intervals_for_stream()` overwrites all individual message intervals in that stream group. So the rate set by MAVSDK gets silently clobbered.

Confirmed by ArduPilot issues: ArduPilot/ardupilot#17046, ArduPilot/ardupilot#19761, ArduPilot/ardupilot#28550.

**Workarounds:**
- Set `MAVn_OPTIONS` bit 2 (NOSTREAMOVERRIDE) on the ArduPilot port used by MAVSDK
- Ensure no other GCS sends `REQUEST_DATA_STREAM` on the same link
- When using SITL with MAVProxy, start with `--streamrate=-1`

This is not a MAVSDK bug — it's a user configuration issue on the ArduPilot side.
Oh, this makes more sense. Thanks for investigating @PavelGuzenfeld. I'll close this issue then.

title: Decide how to pass callbacks to API
author: julianoes
body:
I see that we have inconsistency in the way callbacks are passed into the C++ API.

Some of the APIs use pass-by-value:
```
void subscribe_plugin_something(const subscribe_plugin_something_callback_t callback);
```

Others use pass-by-reference:
```
void subscribe_plugin_something(const subscribe_plugin_something_callback_t &callback);
```

From my understanding, pass-by-value leads to a copy (shallow or deep?) of the function object and therefore adds overhead, however, it prevents the case where the passed callback goes out of scope which can lead to a segfault.

@shakthi-prashanth-m @JonasVautherin opinions?
body_code_blocks: void subscribe_plugin_something(const subscribe_plugin_something_callback_t callback);
void subscribe_plugin_something(const subscribe_plugin_something_callback_t &callback);
resolution_evidence: thread converges on a working answer

answer_comments.body:
I would pass by value as well. I found [this answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/18366273/1368342) very interesting, including:

> That store makes passing by value more optimal. If there is any possibility you are storing a copy of the std::function, pass by value. Otherwise, either way is roughly equivalent: the only downside to by-value is if you are taking the same bulky std::function and having one sub method after another use it. Barring that, a move will be as efficient as a const&.
Do we have to use `std::move` anywhere or does that happen automatically?
From what I understand, it happens automatically. Otherwise it would really not be practical...
This has changed in the meantime anyway, and it seems to work well enough.

title: Camera range options not supported
author: julianoes
body:
We should support camera settings that are not an enum option but rather a range.

An example for such a param can be found in the camera manager:

https://github.com/Dronecode/camera-manager/blob/eef47667506eb97e6ee7349489b7738a825dae14/samples/def/camera-def-uvc.xml#L57-L59

answer_comments.body: `SubscribeRangeSettings`? I see the problem, what do you do with the types.

> SubscribeRangeSettings? I see the problem, what do you do with the types.

Exactly. In Java/Swift, we get a stream of one type. Having a supertype (`Object` or `Any`) is quite similar to having a `String`, in the end.

The camera knows that type it wants for each param, so it can check it and return an error for a wrong argument. Which is probably already the case for, say, a range: if I need an `int` betweeen 0 and 10 and I send 15, the camera will complain (`WRONG_ARGUMENT`?). I don't see a problem with doing that as well if I send "fifteen plz".

Same on the client side, when receiving a value. I don't see it as a big problem if users receive "8" (string) and need to cast it to 8 (int) themselves, given that the camera should never send an invalid value like "eight, I think" (string).

That's not the most beautiful interface ever, but if it contains the information needed to write a dynamic interface on the client side while being auto-generated on the SDK side, I believe it is not too bad.

I would be interested in @byuarus and @douglaswsilva opinions, as they have implemented a client side (not yet for the ranges, obviously).

I'm almost convinced :smile:.

One more thing: I think we also need to be able to specify the interval, so what about:

If `is_range == true`, then `repeated Option options` must contain 2 options with `option_value` set respectively to [min, max] or 3 options with `option_value` set respectively to [min, interval, max].

That would make sense to me :+1:.

Possibly we should also provide the type of the values, in case the client needs that? Let's wait for @byuarus and @douglaswsilva for that, maybe :laughing:.

linked_prs.title: Support for range-based params in camera plugin

comments.body: @JonasVautherin we'll have to figure out the proto for this first, I think.
Agreed. Is it already needed for a camera we support?
It's used a lot in camera-manager, so it's something needed for https://github.com/Auterion/mavlink-testing-suite which tests against camera-manager.
Hm, that's a bit tricky if you ask me but would be one way.

What would be an easier way? Whatever else I can think of implies adding messages per type, and that ends up giving stuff like `SubscribeIntSettings`, `SubscribeEnumSettings`, ... We cannot do fancy `OneOf` or stuff like that, because in the end we have to be able to translate that to all the languages we support.
`SubscribeRangeSettings`? I see the problem, what do you do with the types.

> SubscribeRangeSettings? I see the problem, what do you do with the types.

Exactly. In Java/Swift, we get a stream of one type. Having a supertype (`Object` or `Any`) is quite similar to having a `String`, in the end.

The camera knows that type it wants for each param, so it can check it and return an error for a wrong argument. Which is probably already the case for, say, a range: if I need an `int` betweeen 0 and 10 and I send 15, the camera will complain (`WRONG_ARGUMENT`?). I don't see a problem with doing that as well if I send "fifteen plz".

Same on the client side, when receiving a value. I don't see it as a big problem if users receive "8" (string) and need to cast it to 8 (int) themselves, given that the camera should never send an invalid value like "eight, I think" (string).

That's not the most beautiful interface ever, but if it contains the information needed to write a dynamic interface on the client side while being auto-generated on the SDK side, I believe it is not too bad.

I would be interested in @byuarus and @douglaswsilva opinions, as they have implemented a client side (not yet for the ranges, obviously).

I'm almost convinced :smile:.

One more thing: I think we also need to be able to specify the interval, so what about:

If `is_range == true`, then `repeated Option options` must contain 2 options with `option_value` set respectively to [min, max] or 3 options with `option_value` set respectively to [min, interval, max].

That would make sense to me :+1:.

Possibly we should also provide the type of the values, in case the client needs that? Let's wait for @byuarus and @douglaswsilva for that, maybe :laughing:.

> Possibly we should also provide the type of the values, in case the client needs that? 

@JonasVautherin Yes, you're right. We need this :) 

> If is_range == true, then repeated Option options must contain 2 options with option_value set respectively to [min, max] or 3 options with option_value set respectively to [min, interval, max].

@julianoes  This will work for us.

Currently, for Sony R10C camera, we receive a json file with all possible settings. For R10C they provide the range as an enum, this will work for us too. I would say that it's preferred way of presenting range settings as it will make less likely that client-side will send some weird values. It will save from issues with value type conversions (String/Int/Float/Double) from the UI layer to SDK.

Example of JSON file:
[cameraSettingsJSON.txt](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/files/3394403/cameraSettingsJSON.txt)

Both MAVSDK and gRPC should use the version found by CMake, which is OpenSSL v3 when using the superbuild.

comments.body: I can't believe MAVLink are only letting us have six cameras https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#MAV_COMP_ID_CAMERA :-)

@julianoes 
>I disagree with these API's though because the component ids don't really need to be exposed.

If application is interested in a particular camera (say, downward facing camera), then it needs to be differentiated it by unique camera ID. Can't we use component IDs as camera IDs to differentiate ?

Suppose that a system(vehicle) has 6 cameras, an application may access to camera 1 & 2 as below:
```cpp
DroneCore dc;
...
auto camera_ids = dc.camera_ids(); // similar to device_uuids() method.

// Assuming we've have Camera plugin which is instantiated as below:
auto camera1 = std::make_shared<Camera>(&dc.camera(camera_ids[0]); // access to camera 1
auto camera2 = std::make_shared<Camera>(&dc.camera(camera_ids[1]); // access to camera 2
...
```

I think the API needs to be as simple and clean as possible and therefore I push back on complexity unless absolutely needed. DroneCore could allow to access different cameras but it should be an abstracted API and not the mavlink one.

Ok I agree to keep API as much simple possible. I want to understand what is the complexity in above code.
With current DroneCore interface, we query the device UUIDs that are connected. As we know UUID is per vehicle or system, we need a scheme to distinguish components in a system. If you prefer not to use MAVLink component id, what is the alternative?
We query the devices by UUID. We need to change this so that we get access to the exact component of the system.
So application should make a first call to get UUID list and then make another to get all the components of it.
This is what the above code is trying to do. Do you have a better idea ?
Let's follow up with the discussion in #310, this is getting confusing.

title: MAV_RESULT_IN_PROGRESS: Sigfault when multiple IN_PROGRESS messages are sent before arming
author: RaubCamaioni
body:
Drone Device: Skydio X2

When sending arming commands to the Skydio X2, it performs a long warm-up routine.
While the warm-up routine is running, MAV_RESULT_IN_PROGRESS messages are sent.
When the drone is finished warming up it returns a MAV_RESULT_ACCEPTED message.

This state flow is represented in MAVSDK/src/mavsdk/core/mavlink_command_sender.cpp.

Whenever the second MAV_RESULT_IN_PROGRESS is sent, I get a Sigfault from mavsdk.
It occurs when freeing the memory of a promise. 
 
The "call_callback(temp_callback, temp_result.first, temp_result.second);" function inside  
"MavlinkCommandSender::receive_command_ack(mavlink_message_t message)" is the start of the error stack.  

Does the dev team have any drones that return MAV_RESULT_IN_PROGRESS messages before success when arming?
Is this an expected working feature. 
The workflow does not work for the Skydio X2.

Inside MAVSDK/src/mavsdk/core/mavlink_command_sender.cpp:
All other case statement flows remove the job from the queue: "_work_queue.erase(it)"
Likely, any job that reaches the call_callback function twice will cause a Sigfault. 
The only jobs able to go through the case statement twice are jobs that are returned a PROGRESS message.

Current mitigation: Disabling call_callback for any Progress message. 
Mavlink seems to work perfectly fine with call_callback disabled for Progress message, must not be used anywhere crucial. 

```
        if (temp_callback != nullptr) {
            if (temp_result.first != Result::InProgress)
            {
                call_callback(temp_callback, temp_result.first, temp_result.second);
            }
        }
```

answer_comments.body:
I think you're right. We should ignore `InProgress` here:

https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/23517a00c9395cae8ddf5a31cbd81596cc08309a/src/mavsdk/plugins/action/action_impl.cpp#L246

Do you want to create a pull request? We should probably fix it for all commands in `ActionImpl`.

For some background, this has not come up because PX4 and ArduPilot don't send `ACK_IN_PROGRESS` which has really only been adopted later by cameras etc.

This turned out to be quite easy to fix: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/2320

I haven't tested it, so it would be great if you could give it a quick check.
